Old John of Gaunt, time-honoured Lancaster, / Hast thou, according to thy oath and band, / Brought hither Henry Hereford thy bold son, / Here to make good the boisterous late appeal, / Which then our leisure would not let us hear, / Against the Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Mowbray?

Old John of Gaunt, honoured Duke of Lancaster, have you, as you swore and promised, brought your bold son Henry Hereford here to prove the angry accusation he made recently against the Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Mowbray, which I had no time to hear then?
Tell me, moreover, hast thou sounded him / If he appeal the Duke on ancient malice, / Or worthily, as a good subject should, / On some known ground of treachery in him?
Tell me also: have you found out from him whether he accuses the Duke out of some old grudge, or rightly, as a good subject should, on clear evidence of treason?
As near as I could sift him on that argument, / On some apparent danger seen in him / Aim'd at your Highness, no inveterate malice.
As far as I could get it out of him on that point, it is because of some obvious danger he has seen threatening your Highness, not any long-held hatred.

Then call them to our presence: face to face / And frowning brow to brow, ourselves will hear / The accuser and the accused freely speak. / High-stomach'd are they both and full of ire, / In rage, deaf as the sea, hasty as fire.

Then call them before me. Face to face and frowning brow to brow, I will hear the accuser and the accused speak freely. They are both proud and full of anger; in their rage they are as deaf as the sea and as hasty as fire.
Many years of happy days befall / My gracious sovereign, my most loving liege!
May my gracious king, my most loving lord, have many years of happy days!
Each day still better other's happiness / Until the heavens, envying earth's good hap, / Add an immortal title to your crown!
May each day bring you more happiness than the last, until heaven, envying earth's good fortune, adds an immortal title to your crown!

We thank you both; yet one but flatters us, / As well appeareth by the cause you come; / Namely, to appeal each other of high treason. / Cousin of Hereford, what dost thou object / Against the Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Mowbray?

I thank you both. But one of you is only flattering me, as the reason you have come makes clear: to accuse each other of high treason. Cousin Hereford, what charge do you bring against the Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Mowbray?

First,—heaven be the record to my speech!— / In the devotion of a subject's love, / Tendering the precious safety of my prince, / And free from other misbegotten hate, / Come I appellant to this princely presence. / Now, Thomas Mowbray, do I turn to thee, / And mark my greeting well; for what I speak / My body shall make good upon this earth, / Or my divine soul answer it in heaven. / Thou art a traitor and a miscreant; / Too good to be so and too bad to live, / Since the more fair and crystal is the sky, / The uglier seem the clouds that in it fly. / Once more, the more to aggravate the note, / With a foul traitor's name stuff I thy throat; / And wish, so please my sovereign, ere I move, / What my tongue speaks, my right drawn sword may prove.

First, and may heaven witness what I say, I come here to accuse him before my prince out of a subject's loving duty, out of care for my king's precious safety, and free of any other, unworthy hatred. Now, Thomas Mowbray, I turn to you. Note well how I greet you, because what I say my body will prove here on earth, or my immortal soul will answer for it in heaven. You are a traitor and a villain, too noble to be one and too wicked to live. The clearer and brighter the sky, the uglier the clouds that fly across it look. And to stress the charge, I'll stuff the name of foul traitor down your throat once more. With my king's permission, before I leave here I want my drawn sword to prove what my tongue says.

Let not my cold words here accuse my zeal: / 'Tis not the trial of a woman's war, / The bitter clamour of two eager tongues, / Can arbitrate this cause betwixt us twain; / The blood is hot that must be cool'd for this. / Yet can I not of such tame patience boast / As to be hush'd and nought at all to say. / First, the fair reverence of your highness curbs me / From giving reins and spurs to my free speech; / Which else would post until it had return'd / These terms of treason doubled down his throat. / Setting aside his high blood's royalty, / And let him be no kinsman to my liege, / I do defy him, and I spit at him, / Call him a slanderous coward and a villain: / Which to maintain, I would allow him odds / And meet him, were I tied to run afoot / Even to the frozen ridges of the Alps, / Or any other ground inhabitable, / Wherever Englishman durst set his foot. / Meantime let this defend my loyalty: / By all my hopes, most falsely doth he lie.

Don't judge my loyalty by how coolly I speak. A shouting match like two women quarrelling, two bitter, eager tongues, can't settle this matter between us. Hot blood must be spilled and cooled to do that. But I can't boast of such tame patience as to keep quiet and say nothing at all. First, my respect for your Highness holds me back from giving my speech free rein; otherwise it would gallop on until it had driven these charges of treason back down his throat twice over. Setting aside his royal blood, and pretending he is no relation of my king, I defy him and spit at him. I call him a slandering coward and a villain. To prove it I would give him the advantage and meet him even if I had to run on foot to the frozen ridges of the Alps, or any other place where no one can live, anywhere an Englishman ever dared to set foot. Meanwhile, let this defend my loyalty: by all my hopes, he lies completely.

Pale trembling coward, there I throw my gage, / Disclaiming here the kindred of the king; / And lay aside my high blood's royalty, / Which fear, not reverence, makes thee to except: / If guilty dread have left thee so much strength / As to take up mine honour's pawn, then stoop: / By that, and all the rites of knighthood else, / Will I make good against thee, arm to arm, / What I have spoke or thou canst worst devise.

Pale, trembling coward, there I throw down my glove. I give up any claim to be the king's relative and put aside my royal blood, which you use as an excuse out of fear, not respect. If guilty fear has left you strength enough to pick up the pledge of my honour, then bend down. By that glove, and by all the other rituals of knighthood, I will prove against you in single combat what I have said, or anything worse you can think up.

I take it up; and by that sword I swear / Which gently laid my knighthood on my shoulder, / I'll answer thee in any fair degree, / Or chivalrous design of knightly trial: / And when I mount, alive may I not light / If I be traitor or unjustly fight!

I pick it up. And I swear by the sword that gently laid knighthood on my shoulder that I will answer you in any fair way or any form of knightly combat. And when I mount my horse, may I not get off it alive if I am a traitor or fight unjustly!
What doth our cousin lay to Mowbray's charge? / It must be great that can inherit us / So much as of a thought of ill in him.
What does my cousin accuse Mowbray of? It must be something great to make me even suspect him of anything bad.

Look, what I speak, my life shall prove it true; / That Mowbray hath receiv'd eight thousand nobles / In name of lendings for your highness' soldiers, / The which he hath detain'd for lewd employments, / Like a false traitor and injurious villain. / Besides, I say and will in battle prove, / Or here, or elsewhere to the furthest verge / That ever was survey'd by English eye, / That all the treasons for these eighteen years / Complotted and contrived in this land, / Fetch from false Mowbray their first head and spring. / Further I say, and further will maintain / Upon his bad life to make all this good, / That he did plot the Duke of Gloucester's death, / Suggest his soon-believing adversaries, / And consequently, like a traitor coward, / Sluic'd out his innocent soul through streams of blood: / Which blood, like sacrificing Abel's, cries, / Even from the tongueless caverns of the earth, / To me for justice and rough chastisement; / And, by the glorious worth of my descent, / This arm shall do it, or this life be spent.

Listen: what I say, my life will prove true. Mowbray has received eight thousand gold coins, supposedly as pay for your Highness's soldiers, and has kept them for wicked purposes, like a false traitor and harmful villain. Besides that, I say, and will prove in battle here or anywhere else as far as any English eye has ever seen, that all the treasons plotted and invented in this country in the last eighteen years started with false Mowbray. And I say further, and will prove it on his wicked life, that he plotted the Duke of Gloucester's death, stirred up the Duke's too-trusting enemies, and so, like a traitor and coward, let out his innocent soul in streams of blood. That blood, like the blood of Abel the sacrificer, cries out to me from the silent caves of the earth for justice and harsh punishment. And by my glorious ancestry, this arm will deliver it, or I will die trying.
How high a pitch his resolution soars! / Thomas of Norfolk, what say'st thou to this?
How high his determination flies! Thomas of Norfolk, what do you say to this?
O! let my sovereign turn away his face / And bid his ears a little while be deaf, / Till I have told this slander of his blood / How God and good men hate so foul a liar.
Oh, let my king turn his face away and close his ears for a moment, until I have told this disgrace to his family how much God and good men hate such a foul liar.

Mowbray, impartial are our eyes and ears: / Were he my brother, nay, my kingdom's heir,— / As he is but my father's brother's son,— / Now, by my sceptre's awe I make a vow, / Such neighbour nearness to our sacred blood / Should nothing privilege him nor partialize / The unstooping firmness of my upright soul. / He is our subject, Mowbray; so art thou: / Free speech and fearless I to thee allow.

Mowbray, my eyes and ears are fair to both sides. If he were my brother, or even heir to my kingdom, and he is only my uncle's son, I swear by my royal sceptre that such closeness to my sacred blood would not give him any privilege or bend my firm, upright judgment. He is my subject, Mowbray, and so are you. I allow you to speak freely and without fear.

Then, Bolingbroke, as low as to thy heart, / Through the false passage of thy throat, thou liest. / Three parts of that receipt I had for Calais / Disburs'd I duly to his highness' soldiers; / The other part reserv'd I by consent, / For that my sovereign liege was in my debt / Upon remainder of a dear account, / Since last I went to France to fetch his queen. / Now swallow down that lie. For Gloucester's death, / I slew him not; but to my own disgrace / Neglected my sworn duty in that case. / For you, my noble Lord of Lancaster, / The honourable father to my foe, / Once did I lay an ambush for your life, / A trespass that doth vex my grieved soul; / But ere I last receiv'd the sacrament / I did confess it, and exactly begg'd / Your Grace's pardon; and I hope I had it. / This is my fault: as for the rest appeal'd, / It issues from the rancour of a villain, / A recreant and most degenerate traitor; / Which in myself I boldly will defend, / And interchangeably hurl down my gage / Upon this overweening traitor's foot, / To prove myself a loyal gentleman / Even in the best blood chamber'd in his bosom. / In haste whereof, most heartily I pray / Your highness to assign our trial day.

Then, Bolingbroke, you lie, right down your lying throat to your heart. Of the money I received for Calais, I duly paid three quarters to his Highness's soldiers. The rest I kept back with the King's agreement, because he owed me money left over from a large debt from when I last went to France to bring back his queen. So swallow that lie. As for Gloucester's death, I did not kill him; but to my shame I failed in my sworn duty in that matter. As for you, my noble Lord of Lancaster, honourable father of my enemy: I did once set an ambush to kill you, a crime that troubles my grieving soul. But before I last took communion I confessed it and begged your Grace's pardon, and I hope I received it. That is my fault. The rest of the charges come from the hatred of a villain, a coward and a most degenerate traitor. I will boldly defend myself against them, and in return I throw my glove down at this arrogant traitor's foot, to prove myself a loyal gentleman by spilling the best blood in his heart. To hurry that on, I beg your Highness with all my heart to set the day of our combat.

Wrath-kindled gentlemen, be rul'd by me; / Let's purge this choler without letting blood: / This we prescribe, though no physician; / Deep malice makes too deep incision: / Forget, forgive; conclude and be agreed, / Our doctors say this is no month to bleed. / Good uncle, let this end where it begun; / We'll calm the Duke of Norfolk, you your son.

You angry gentlemen, do as I say. Let's get rid of this rage without shedding blood. This is my prescription, though I am no doctor: deep hatred cuts too deep. Forget, forgive, end it and agree; our doctors say this is not the month for bleeding. Good uncle, let this end where it began. I'll calm the Duke of Norfolk, you calm your son.
To be a make-peace shall become my age: / Throw down, my son, the Duke of Norfolk's gage.
Being a peacemaker suits my age. My son, throw down the Duke of Norfolk's glove.
When, Harry, when? / Obedience bids I should not bid again.
Well, Harry, well? Obedience means I shouldn't have to ask you twice.
Norfolk, throw down; we bid; / There is no boot.
Norfolk, throw it down. I order it. There's no use resisting.

Myself I throw, dread sovereign, at thy foot. / My life thou shalt command, but not my shame: / The one my duty owes; but my fair name,— / Despite of death, that lives upon my grave,— / To dark dishonour's use thou shalt not have. / I am disgrac'd, impeach'd, and baffled here; / Pierc'd to the soul with slander's venom'd spear, / The which no balm can cure but his heart-blood / Which breath'd this poison.

I throw myself at your feet, my feared king. You may command my life, but not my shame. My life I owe to you as my duty; but my good name, which will live on my grave in spite of death, you will not have for dark dishonour. I am disgraced, accused and humiliated here, stabbed to the soul with the poisoned spear of slander. No medicine can cure it except the blood from the heart of the man who breathed out this poison.
Rage must be withstood: / Give me his gage: lions make leopards tame.
Your anger must be held back. Give me his glove. Lions tame leopards.

Yea, but not change his spots: take but my shame, / And I resign my gage. My dear dear lord, / The purest treasure mortal times afford / Is spotless reputation; that away, / Men are but gilded loam or painted clay. / A jewel in a ten-times barr'd-up chest / Is a bold spirit in a loyal breast. / Mine honour is my life; both grow in one; / Take honour from me, and my life is done: / Then, dear my liege, mine honour let me try; / In that I live, and for that will I die.

Yes, but they don't change their spots. Take away my shame and I'll give up the glove. My dear, dear lord, the purest treasure this life offers is a spotless reputation. Without it, men are just gilded mud or painted clay. A bold spirit in a loyal heart is a jewel in a chest locked ten times over. My honour is my life; the two grow together as one. Take my honour away and my life is over. So, my dear lord, let me put my honour to the test. I live for it, and I will die for it.
Cousin, throw down your gage: do you begin.
Cousin, throw down your glove. You start.

O! God defend my soul from such deep sin. / Shall I seem crest-fall'n in my father's sight, / Or with pale beggar-fear impeach my height / Before this outdar'd dastard? Ere my tongue / Shall wound my honour with such feeble wrong / Or sound so base a parle, my teeth shall tear / The slavish motive of recanting fear, / And spit it bleeding in his high disgrace, / Where shame doth harbour, even in Mowbray's face.

Oh, God keep my soul from such a terrible sin! Should I look defeated in my father's sight, or lower my rank with cowardly fear in front of this beaten coward? Before my tongue wounds my honour with such weakness or calls such a shameful truce, my teeth will tear out the cowardly tongue that would take it back and spit it, bleeding, at the place where shame lives: in Mowbray's face.

We were not born to sue, but to command: / Which since we cannot do to make you friends, / Be ready, as your lives shall answer it, / At Coventry, upon Saint Lambert's day: / There shall your swords and lances arbitrate / The swelling difference of your settled hate: / Since we can not atone you, we shall see / Justice design the victor's chivalry. / Lord Marshal, command our officers-at-arms / Be ready to direct these home alarms.

I was not born to plead, but to command. Since I can't make you friends, be ready, on pain of death, at Coventry on St Lambert's Day. There your swords and lances will settle the swelling difference of your fixed hatred. Since I cannot reconcile you, we'll see justice declare the winner by knightly combat. Lord Marshal, order my heralds to be ready to manage this quarrel at home.

Alas, the part I had in Woodstock's blood / Doth more solicit me than your exclaims, / To stir against the butchers of his life. / But since correction lieth in those hands / Which made the fault that we cannot correct, / Put we our quarrel to the will of heaven; / Who, when they see the hours ripe on earth, / Will rain hot vengeance on offenders' heads.

Alas, being Woodstock's brother moves me more than your cries do to act against the butchers who killed him. But since the power to punish lies in the hands of the very man who committed the crime, which we cannot punish, let us leave our quarrel to the will of heaven. When heaven sees the time is ripe on earth, it will rain hot vengeance on the heads of the guilty.

Finds brotherhood in thee no sharper spur? / Hath love in thy old blood no living fire? / Edward's seven sons, whereof thyself art one, / Were as seven vials of his sacred blood, / Or seven fair branches springing from one root: / Some of those seven are dried by nature's course, / Some of those branches by the Destinies cut; / But Thomas, my dear lord, my life, my Gloucester, / One vial full of Edward's sacred blood, / One flourishing branch of his most royal root, / Is crack'd, and all the precious liquor spilt; / Is hack'd down, and his summer leaves all vaded, / By envy's hand and murder's bloody axe. / Ah, Gaunt! his blood was thine: that bed, that womb, / That metal, that self-mould, that fashion'd thee, / Made him a man; and though thou liv'st and breath'st, / Yet art thou slain in him: thou dost consent / In some large measure to thy father's death / In that thou seest thy wretched brother die, / Who was the model of thy father's life. / Call it not patience, Gaunt; it is despair: / In suffering thus thy brother to be slaughter'd, / Thou showest the naked pathway to thy life, / Teaching stern murder how to butcher thee: / That which in mean men we entitle patience / Is pale cold cowardice in noble breasts. / What shall I say? To safeguard thine own life, / The best way is to venge my Gloucester's death.

Doesn't being his brother spur you on more sharply than that? Is there no living fire of love in your old blood? Edward's seven sons, and you are one of them, were like seven bottles of his sacred blood, or seven fine branches growing from one root. Some of the seven have dried up naturally; some of the branches have been cut by fate. But Thomas, my dear husband, my life, my Gloucester, one bottle full of Edward's sacred blood, one flourishing branch of his royal root, has been cracked and all its precious liquid spilled, has been hacked down and all his summer leaves faded, by the hand of malice and the bloody axe of murder. Ah, Gaunt, his blood was yours! The same bed, the same womb, the same metal and the same mould that made you made him a man. Though you live and breathe, you are killed in him. You partly agree to your own father's death by watching your poor brother die, who was the image of your father's life. Don't call it patience, Gaunt; it is despair. By letting your brother be slaughtered like this, you show the open road to your own life and teach cruel murder how to butcher you. What we call patience in common men is pale, cold cowardice in noble ones. What more can I say? The best way to protect your own life is to avenge my Gloucester's death.

God's is the quarrel; for God's substitute, / His deputy anointed in his sight, / Hath caus'd his death; the which if wrongfully, / Let heaven revenge, for I may never lift / An angry arm against his minister.

This quarrel belongs to God. God's representative, his deputy anointed in his sight, caused Gloucester's death. If it was wrong, let heaven take revenge, because I can never raise an angry arm against God's minister.
Where then, alas! may I complain myself?
Then who, alas, can I complain to?
To God, the widow's champion and defence.
To God, the protector and defender of widows.

Why then, I will. Farewell, old Gaunt. / Thou go'st to Coventry, there to behold / Our cousin Hereford and fell Mowbray fight: / O! sit my husband's wrongs on Hereford's spear, / That it may enter butcher Mowbray's breast. / Or, if misfortune miss the first career, / Be Mowbray's sins so heavy in his bosom / That they may break his foaming courser's back, / And throw the rider headlong in the lists, / A caitiff recreant to my cousin Hereford! / Farewell, old Gaunt: thy sometimes brother's wife / With her companion, Grief, must end her life.

Then I will. Goodbye, old Gaunt. You are going to Coventry to watch our cousin Hereford and cruel Mowbray fight. Oh, may my husband's wrongs ride on Hereford's spear, so that it goes into butcher Mowbray's heart! Or if bad luck makes him miss at the first charge, may Mowbray's sins be so heavy in his heart that they break his foaming horse's back and throw the rider headlong into the arena, a cowardly wretch at my cousin Hereford's mercy! Goodbye, old Gaunt. Your dead brother's wife must end her life with her only companion, grief.
Sister, farewell; I must to Coventry. / As much good stay with thee as go with me!
Sister, goodbye. I must go to Coventry. May as much good stay with you as goes with me!

Yet one word more. Grief boundeth where it falls, / Not with the empty hollowness, but weight: / I take my leave before I have begun, / For sorrow ends not when it seemeth done. / Commend me to thy brother, Edmund York. / Lo! this is all: nay, yet depart not so; / Though this be all, do not so quickly go; / I shall remember more. Bid him—ah, what?— / With all good speed at Plashy visit me. / Alack! and what shall good old York there see / But empty lodgings and unfurnish'd walls, / Unpeopled offices, untrodden stones? / And what hear there for welcome but my groans? / Therefore commend me; let him not come there, / To seek out sorrow that dwells every where. / Desolate, desolate, will I hence and die: / The last leave of thee takes my weeping eye.

One more word. Grief bounces back where it falls, not because it is hollow but because it is heavy. I'm saying goodbye before I've even begun, because sorrow doesn't end when it seems to be over. Give my regards to your brother, Edmund of York. There, that's all. No, don't leave yet; even if that's all, don't go so quickly. I'll remember more. Tell him... ah, what? To visit me at Plashy as soon as he can. Alas, and what will good old York see there but empty rooms and bare walls, deserted servants' quarters and stones nobody walks on? And what welcome will he hear there but my groans? So give him my regards, but don't let him come there looking for sorrow; it is everywhere. Desolate, desolate, I will go away and die. My weeping eye takes its last look at you.
My Lord Aumerle, is Harry Hereford arm'd?
My Lord Aumerle, is Harry Hereford armed?
Yea, at all points; and longs to enter in.
Yes, completely, and he is eager to come in.
The Duke of Norfolk, sprightfully and bold, / Stays but the summons of the appelant's trumpet.
The Duke of Norfolk, full of spirit and courage, is only waiting for the challenger's trumpet to call him.
Why then, the champions are prepar'd, and stay / For nothing but his Majesty's approach.
Then both champions are ready, and are waiting for nothing but his Majesty's arrival.
Marshal, demand of yonder champion / The cause of his arrival here in arms: / Ask him his name, and orderly proceed / To swear him in the justice of his cause.
Marshal, ask that champion over there why he has come here armed. Ask him his name, and then, in due order, make him swear that his cause is just.

In God's name and the king's, say who thou art, / And why thou comest thus knightly clad in arms, / Against what man thou comest, and what thy quarrel. / Speak truly, on thy knighthood and thy oath; / As so defend thee heaven and thy valour!

In the name of God and the King, say who you are, why you come here dressed in armour like a knight, whom you have come to fight and what your quarrel is. Speak truthfully, on your knighthood and your oath, and may heaven and your courage defend you!

My name is Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk, / Who hither come engaged by my oath,— / Which God defend a knight should violate!— / Both to defend my loyalty and truth / To God, my King, and my succeeding issue, / Against the Duke of Hereford that appeals me; / And, by the grace of God and this mine arm, / To prove him, in defending of myself, / A traitor to my God, my King, and me: / And as I truly fight, defend me heaven!

My name is Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk. I come here bound by my oath, which God forbid a knight should break, to defend my loyalty and faithfulness to God, my King and my descendants against the Duke of Hereford, who accuses me. And by the grace of God and this arm of mine, I come to prove, by defending myself, that he is a traitor to my God, my King and me. And as I fight honestly, may heaven defend me!
Marshal, ask yonder knight in arms, / Both who he is and why he cometh hither / Thus plated in habiliments of war; / And formally, according to our law, / Depose him in the justice of his cause.
Marshal, ask that armed knight over there who he is and why he comes here dressed in armour for war. And formally, as our law requires, take his oath that his cause is just.
What is thy name? and wherefore com'st thou hither / Before King Richard in his royal lists? / Against whom comest thou? and what's thy quarrel? / Speak like a true knight, so defend thee heaven!
What is your name? Why have you come here, before King Richard in his royal arena? Whom have you come to fight, and what is your quarrel? Speak like a true knight, and may heaven defend you!

Harry of Hereford, Lancaster, and Derby, / Am I; who ready here do stand in arms, / To prove by God's grace and my body's valour, / In lists, on Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk, / That he's a traitor foul and dangerous, / To God of heaven, King Richard, and to me: / And as I truly fight, defend me heaven!

I am Harry of Hereford, Lancaster and Derby. I stand here armed and ready to prove in combat, by God's grace and my body's courage, against Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk, that he is a foul and dangerous traitor to God in heaven, to King Richard and to me. And as I fight honestly, may heaven defend me!
On pain of death, no person be so bold / Or daring-hardy as to touch the lists, / Except the Marshal and such officers / Appointed to direct these fair designs.
On pain of death, let no one be so bold or reckless as to touch the barriers of the arena, except the Marshal and the officers appointed to manage this honourable contest.

Lord Marshal, let me kiss my sovereign's hand, / And bow my knee before his Majesty: / For Mowbray and myself are like two men / That vow a long and weary pilgrimage; / Then let us take a ceremonious leave / And loving farewell of our several friends.

Lord Marshal, let me kiss my king's hand and kneel before his Majesty. Mowbray and I are like two men who have vowed to go on a long and weary pilgrimage, so let us take a formal leave and say a loving goodbye to our friends.
The appellant in all duty greets your highness, / And craves to kiss your hand and take his leave.
The challenger respectfully greets your Highness and asks to kiss your hand and say goodbye.

[Descends from his throne] We will descend and fold him in our arms. / Cousin of Hereford, as thy cause is right, / So be thy fortune in this royal fight! / Farewell, my blood; which if to-day thou shed, / Lament we may, but not revenge thee dead.

I will come down and take him in my arms. Cousin Hereford, may your fortune in this royal fight be as good as your cause is just! Goodbye, my own blood. If you shed it today, I may mourn you, but I may not avenge your death.

O! let no noble eye profane a tear / For me, if I be gor'd with Mowbray's spear. / As confident as is the falcon's flight / Against a bird, do I with Mowbray fight. / My loving lord, I take my leave of you; / Of you, my noble cousin, Lord Aumerle; / Not sick, although I have to do with death, / But lusty, young, and cheerly drawing breath. / Lo! as at English feasts, so I regreet / The daintiest last, to make the end most sweet: / O thou, the earthly author of my blood, / Whose youthful spirit, in me regenerate, / Doth with a twofold vigour lift me up / To reach at victory above my head, / Add proof unto mine armour with thy prayers, / And with thy blessings steel my lance's point, / That it may enter Mowbray's waxen coat, / And furbish new the name of John a Gaunt, / Even in the lusty haviour of his son.

Oh, let no noble eye waste a tear on me if I am pierced by Mowbray's spear. I fight Mowbray as confidently as a falcon flies at a bird. My loving lord, I say goodbye to you; and to you, my noble cousin, Lord Aumerle. I am not sick, though I am dealing with death, but strong, young and breathing cheerfully. Look, as at English feasts, I greet the sweetest dish last, to make the end the best. Oh, you, my father on earth, whose young spirit, reborn in me, lifts me up with double strength to reach for a victory above my head: strengthen my armour with your prayers, and harden my lance's point with your blessings, so that it pierces Mowbray's armour as if it were wax and polishes up the name of John of Gaunt again through the vigorous deeds of his son.

God in thy good cause make thee prosperous! / Be swift like lightning in the execution; / And let thy blows, doubly redoubled, / Fall like amazing thunder on the casque / Of thy adverse pernicious enemy: / Rouse up thy youthful blood, be valiant, and live.

May God make you succeed in your good cause! Be as quick as lightning in the fight, and let your blows, doubled and doubled again, fall like stunning thunder on the helmet of your destructive enemy. Stir up your young blood, be brave, and live.
Mine innocency and Saint George to thrive!
May my innocence and Saint George help me win!

[Rising] However God or fortune cast my lot, / There lives or dies, true to King Richard's throne, / A loyal, just, and upright gentleman. / Never did captive with a freer heart / Cast off his chains of bondage and embrace / His golden uncontroll'd enfranchisement, / More than my dancing soul doth celebrate / This feast of battle with mine adversary. / Most mighty liege, and my companion peers, / Take from my mouth the wish of happy years. / As gentle and as jocund as to jest / Go I to fight: truth hath a quiet breast.

However God or fortune decides my fate, there lives or dies here a loyal, just and honest gentleman, faithful to King Richard's throne. No prisoner ever threw off his chains and welcomed his golden, unlimited freedom with a happier heart than my dancing soul feels as it celebrates this feast of battle with my enemy. Most mighty lord, and my fellow noblemen, accept my wish that you may have many happy years. I go to fight as calmly and cheerfully as if I were going to a game. A clear conscience has a peaceful heart.
Farewell, my lord: securely I espy / Virtue with valour couched in thine eye. / Order the trial, Marshal, and begin.
Goodbye, my lord. I can see clearly that goodness and courage lie together in your eyes. Organise the combat, Marshal, and begin.
Harry of Hereford, Lancaster, and Derby, / Receive thy lance; and God defend the right!
Harry of Hereford, Lancaster and Derby, take your lance, and may God defend the right!
[Rising] Strong as a tower in hope, I cry 'amen'.
Strong as a tower in my hope, I say 'Amen'.
[To an officer] Go bear this lance to Thomas, / Duke of Norfolk.
Take this lance to Thomas, Duke of Norfolk.

Harry of Hereford, Lancaster, and Derby, / Stands here for God, his sovereign, and himself, / On pain to be found false and recreant, / To prove the Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Mowbray, / A traitor to his God, his King, and him; / And dares him to set forward to the fight.

Harry of Hereford, Lancaster and Derby stands here for God, his king and himself, ready to prove, on pain of being found a liar and a coward, that the Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Mowbray, is a traitor to his God, his King and himself. He dares him to come forward and fight.

Here standeth Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk, / On pain to be found false and recreant, / Both to defend himself, and to approve / Henry of Hereford, Lancaster, and Derby, / To God, his sovereign, and to him disloyal; / Courageously and with a free desire, / Attending but the signal to begin.

Here stands Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk, ready, on pain of being found a liar and a coward, to defend himself and to prove that Henry of Hereford, Lancaster and Derby is disloyal to God, his king and him. He comes with courage and eagerness, waiting only for the signal to begin.
Sound trumpets; and set forward, combatants.
Sound the trumpets, and charge, combatants.
Stay, the King hath thrown his warder down.
Stop! The King has thrown down his staff.
Let them lay by their helmets and their spears, / And both return back to their chairs again: / Withdraw with us; and let the trumpets sound / While we return these dukes what we decree.
Let them put aside their helmets and spears, and both go back to their seats. Come away with me, and let the trumpets sound while I return to tell these dukes what I have decided.

[To the Combatants] Draw near, / And list what with our council we have done. / For that our kingdom's earth should not be soil'd / With that dear blood which it hath fostered; / And for our eyes do hate the dire aspect / Of civil wounds plough'd up with neighbours' swords; / And for we think the eagle-winged pride / Of sky-aspiring and ambitious thoughts, / With rival-hating envy, set on you / To wake our peace, which in our country's cradle / Draws the sweet infant breath of gentle sleep; / Which so rous'd up with boist'rous untun'd drums, / With harsh-resounding trumpets' dreadful bray, / And grating shock of wrathful iron arms, / Might from our quiet confines fright fair peace / And make us wade even in our kindred's blood: / Therefore we banish you our territories: / You, cousin Hereford, upon pain of life, / Till twice five summers have enrich'd our fields / Shall not regreet our fair dominions, / But tread the stranger paths of banishment.

Come closer, and listen to what my council and I have decided. Because the soil of my kingdom should not be stained with the precious blood it has brought up, and because my eyes hate the terrible sight of wounds of civil war, ploughed open by neighbours' swords, and because I think that the proud, high-flying ambition that aims at the sky, together with jealous rivalry, set you on to wake up peace, which lies in our country's cradle breathing the sweet breath of a sleeping baby; and that peace, woken by loud, tuneless drums, the harsh, dreadful blare of trumpets and the grating clash of angry weapons, might be frightened out of our quiet land and make us wade in the blood of our own relatives: for these reasons I banish you from my lands. You, cousin Hereford, on pain of death, shall not see my fair kingdom again until ten summers have ripened our fields, but shall walk the foreign roads of exile.
Your will be done. This must my comfort be, / That sun that warms you here shall shine on me; / And those his golden beams to you here lent / Shall point on me and gild my banishment.
Your will be done. My comfort must be this: the same sun that warms you here will shine on me, and the golden beams it lends you here will fall on me and turn my exile to gold.

Norfolk, for thee remains a heavier doom, / Which I with some unwillingness pronounce: / The sly slow hours shall not determinate / The dateless limit of thy dear exile; / The hopeless word of 'never to return' / Breathe I against thee, upon pain of life.

Norfolk, a heavier sentence remains for you, which I announce with some reluctance. The slow, creeping hours will not bring to an end your exile, which has no end date. I pronounce against you, on pain of death, the hopeless words 'never to return'.

A heavy sentence, my most sovereign liege, / And all unlook'd for from your highness' mouth: / A dearer merit, not so deep a maim / As to be cast forth in the common air, / Have I deserved at your highness' hands. / The language I have learn'd these forty years, / My native English, now I must forgo; / And now my tongue's use is to me no more / Than an unstringed viol or a harp, / Or like a cunning instrument cas'd up / Or, being open, put into his hands / That knows no touch to tune the harmony: / Within my mouth you have engaol'd my tongue, / Doubly portcullis'd with my teeth and lips; / And dull, unfeeling, barren ignorance / Is made my gaoler to attend on me. / I am too old to fawn upon a nurse, / Too far in years to be a pupil now: / What is thy sentence, then, but speechless death, / Which robs my tongue from breathing native breath?

A heavy sentence, my most royal lord, and completely unexpected from your Highness's mouth. I have deserved a better reward from your Highness than such a deep wound as to be thrown out into the open world. Now I must give up the language I have learned for forty years, my native English. My tongue is now no more use to me than a viol or harp without strings, or a fine instrument shut in its case, or, if it is opened, put into the hands of someone who has no idea how to play it. You have imprisoned my tongue inside my mouth, behind the double gate of my teeth and lips, and dull, unfeeling, empty ignorance has been made my jailer. I am too old to start learning from a nurse again, too old to be a schoolboy now. So what is your sentence but a speechless death, since it stops my tongue speaking its native language?
It boots thee not to be compassionate: / After our sentence plaining comes too late.
It does you no good to feel sorry for yourself. Complaining comes too late after my sentence.
Then thus I turn me from my country's light, / To dwell in solemn shades of endless night.
Then I turn away from my country's light, to live in the solemn shadows of endless night.

Return again, and take an oath with thee. / Lay on our royal sword your banish'd hands; / Swear by the duty that you owe to God,— / Our part therein we banish with yourselves— / To keep the oath that we administer: / You never shall, so help you truth and God!— / Embrace each other's love in banishment; / Nor never look upon each other's face; / Nor never write, regreet, nor reconcile / This louring tempest of your home-bred hate; / Nor never by advised purpose meet / To plot, contrive, or complot any ill / 'Gainst us, our state, our subjects, or our land.

Come back, and take an oath with you. Lay your banished hands on my royal sword. Swear by the duty you owe to God (the duty you owe me goes into exile with you) that you will keep the oath I now give you: that you will never, so help you truth and God, become friends in exile, nor ever look at each other's faces, nor ever write, greet each other or settle this dark storm of homegrown hatred, nor ever meet on purpose to plot, plan or scheme any harm against me, my government, my subjects or my country.
And I, to keep all this.
And I swear to keep all this.

Norfolk, so far as to mine enemy:— / By this time, had the king permitted us, / One of our souls had wand'red in the air, / Banish'd this frail sepulchre of our flesh, / As now our flesh is banish'd from this land: / Confess thy treasons ere thou fly the realm; / Since thou hast far to go, bear not along / The clogging burden of a guilty soul.

Norfolk, I'll say this much to you as my enemy. By now, if the king had let us, one of our souls would be wandering in the air, banished from the frail tomb of its body, just as our bodies are now banished from this country. Confess your treasons before you leave the kingdom. Since you have a long way to go, don't carry the dragging weight of a guilty soul with you.

No, Bolingbroke: if ever I were traitor, / My name be blotted from the book of life, / And I from heaven banish'd as from hence! / But what thou art, God, thou, and I, do know; / And all too soon, I fear, the king shall rue. / Farewell, my liege. Now no way can I stray; / Save back to England, all the world's my way.

No, Bolingbroke. If I was ever a traitor, may my name be wiped out of the book of life, and may I be banished from heaven as I am from here! But God, you and I know what you are, and I fear the king will regret it all too soon. Goodbye, my lord. Now I can't lose my way: the whole world is my road, except the way back to England.

Uncle, even in the glasses of thine eyes / I see thy grieved heart: thy sad aspect / Hath from the number of his banish'd years / Pluck'd four away.— [To BOLINGBROKE] Six frozen winters spent, / Return with welcome home from banishment.
Uncle, I can see your grieving heart in the mirrors of your eyes. Your sad face has taken four years away from his exile. Come home with a welcome from banishment when six frozen winters have passed.
How long a time lies in one little word! / Four lagging winters and four wanton springs / End in a word: such is the breath of kings.
What a long time lies in one little word! Four slow winters and four playful springs ended in a word. That is the power of a king's breath.

I thank my liege that in regard of me / He shortens four years of my son's exile; / But little vantage shall I reap thereby: / For, ere the six years that he hath to spend / Can change their moons and bring their times about, / My oil-dried lamp and time-bewasted light / Shall be extinct with age and endless night; / My inch of taper will be burnt and done, / And blindfold death not let me see my son.

I thank my lord for shortening my son's exile by four years for my sake. But I won't get much benefit from it. Before the six years he has to spend abroad can change their moons and come round, my lamp, dried of oil, and my light, worn out by time, will be put out by age and endless night. My last inch of candle will burn down, and blindfolded death won't let me see my son.
Why, uncle, thou hast many years to live.
Why, uncle, you have many years to live.

But not a minute, king, that thou canst give: / Shorten my days thou canst with sullen sorrow, / And pluck nights from me, but not lend a morrow; / Thou can'st help time to furrow me with age, / But stop no wrinkle in his pilgrimage; / Thy word is current with him for my death, / But dead, thy kingdom cannot buy my breath.

But not a minute, King, that you can give me. You can shorten my days with gloomy sorrow and steal nights from me, but you can't lend me one tomorrow. You can help time plough me with the lines of age, but you can't stop one wrinkle on its journey. Your word is good enough for time to bring my death; but once I'm dead, your whole kingdom cannot buy back my breath.
Thy son is banish'd upon good advice, / Whereto thy tongue a party-verdict gave. / Why at our justice seem'st thou then to lower?
Your son was banished on good advice, and you yourself gave your vote for it. So why do you seem to frown at my justice?

Things sweet to taste prove in digestion sour. / You urg'd me as a judge; but I had rather / You would have bid me argue like a father. / O! had it been a stranger, not my child, / To smooth his fault I should have been more mild: / A partial slander sought I to avoid, / And in the sentence my own life destroy'd. / Alas! I look'd when some of you should say / I was too strict to make mine own away; / But you gave leave to my unwilling tongue / Against my will to do myself this wrong.

Things that taste sweet turn sour when you digest them. You asked me to speak as a judge, but I would rather you had told me to argue like a father. Oh, if it had been a stranger and not my child, I would have been gentler and played down his fault. I tried to avoid being accused of favouring my son, and by my sentence I destroyed my own life. Alas, I kept waiting for one of you to say I was too strict in sending away my own son. But you allowed my unwilling tongue to do me this harm against my will.
Cousin, farewell; and, uncle, bid him so: / Six years we banish him, and he shall go.
Cousin, goodbye; and, uncle, say goodbye to him. I banish him for six years, and he shall go.
Cousin, farewell: what presence must not know, / From where you do remain let paper show.
Cousin, goodbye. What we can't tell each other face to face, let your letters tell from wherever you are.
My lord, no leave take I; for I will ride, / As far as land will let me, by your side.
My lord, I won't say goodbye yet, because I will ride beside you as far as the land goes.
O! to what purpose dost thou hoard thy words, / That thou return'st no greeting to thy friends?
Oh, why are you saving up your words and not returning your friends' greetings?
I have too few to take my leave of you, / When the tongue's office should be prodigal / To breathe the abundant dolour of the heart.
I have too few words to say goodbye to you, when my tongue should be pouring them out to express the overflowing grief of my heart.
Thy grief is but thy absence for a time.
Your grief is only that you'll be away for a while.
Joy absent, grief is present for that time.
With joy away, grief is here for all that while.
What is six winters? They are quickly gone.
What are six winters? They pass quickly.
To men in joy; but grief makes one hour ten.
For happy men, yes. But grief turns one hour into ten.
Call it a travel that thou tak'st for pleasure.
Think of it as a journey you are taking for pleasure.
My heart will sigh when I miscall it so, / Which finds it an enforced pilgrimage.
My heart will sigh if I call it that, because it feels like a forced pilgrimage.
The sullen passage of thy weary steps / Esteem as foil wherein thou art to set / The precious jewel of thy home return.
Think of the gloomy journey of your weary steps as the setting in which you will place the precious jewel of your return home.

Nay, rather, every tedious stride I make / Will but remember me what a deal of world / I wander from the jewels that I love. / Must I not serve a long apprenticehood / To foreign passages, and in the end, / Having my freedom, boast of nothing else / But that I was a journeyman to grief?

No. Every dull step I take will just remind me how far I am wandering from the jewels I love. Won't I have to serve a long apprenticeship in foreign travel, and in the end, when I am free, be able to boast of nothing except that I was a trained worker in grief?

All places that the eye of heaven visits / Are to a wise man ports and happy havens. / Teach thy necessity to reason thus; / There is no virtue like necessity. / Think not the king did banish thee, / But thou the king. Woe doth the heavier sit, / Where it perceives it is but faintly borne. / Go, say I sent thee forth to purchase honour, / And not the King exil'd thee; or suppose / Devouring pestilence hangs in our air, / And thou art flying to a fresher clime. / Look, what thy soul holds dear, imagine it / To lie that way thou go'st, not whence thou com'st. / Suppose the singing birds musicians, / The grass whereon thou tread'st the presence strew'd, / The flowers fair ladies, and thy steps no more / Than a delightful measure or a dance; / For gnarling sorrow hath less power to bite / The man that mocks at it and sets it light.

To a wise man, every place the sun shines on is a port and a happy harbour. Teach yourself in your hardship to think like this: there is no virtue like accepting what you must. Don't think the King banished you; think that you banished the King. Sorrow sits more heavily on someone who bears it weakly. Go, and say I sent you away to win honour, and the King didn't exile you. Or imagine a deadly plague hanging in our air, and you are escaping to a healthier country. Whatever your soul holds dear, imagine it lies in the direction you are going, not the place you came from. Imagine the singing birds are musicians, the grass you walk on is a royal hall strewn with rushes, the flowers are beautiful ladies and your steps are just a graceful dance. Snarling sorrow has less power to bite a man who laughs at it and takes it lightly.

O! who can hold a fire in his hand / By thinking on the frosty Caucasus? / Or cloy the hungry edge of appetite / By bare imagination of a feast? / Or wallow naked in December snow / By thinking on fantastic summer's heat? / O, no! the apprehension of the good / Gives but the greater feeling to the worse: / Fell sorrow's tooth doth never rankle more / Than when it bites, but lanceth not the sore.

Oh, who can hold fire in his hand by thinking of the frosty Caucasus mountains? Or satisfy the sharp edge of hunger just by imagining a feast? Or roll naked in December snow by thinking of imaginary summer heat? Oh, no! Thinking about good things only makes you feel the bad ones more. Sorrow's cruel tooth never hurts more than when it bites without opening the wound to let it heal.
Come, come, my son, I'll bring thee on thy way. / Had I thy youth and cause, I would not stay.
Come, come, my son, I'll set you on your way. If I had your youth and your reason to go, I wouldn't stay.
Then, England's ground, farewell; sweet soil, adieu; / My mother, and my nurse, that bears me yet! / Where'er I wander, boast of this I can, / Though banish'd, yet a true-born Englishman.
Then, ground of England, goodbye. Sweet soil, farewell, my mother and my nurse, who still carries me! Wherever I wander, I can boast of this: though banished, I am still a true-born Englishman.
We did observe. Cousin Aumerle, / How far brought you high Hereford on his way?
We noticed. Cousin Aumerle, how far did you go with high and mighty Hereford?
I brought high Hereford, if you call him so, / But to the next highway, and there I left him.
I took high Hereford, if you call him that, only as far as the next main road, and left him there.
And say, what store of parting tears were shed?
And tell me, how many tears were shed at parting?
Faith, none for me; except the north-east wind, / Which then blew bitterly against our faces, / Awak'd the sleeping rheum, and so by chance / Did grace our hollow parting with a tear.
Honestly, none from me, except that the north-east wind, which was blowing bitterly in our faces, woke up my watery eyes, and so by chance decorated our insincere parting with a tear.
What said our cousin when you parted with him?
What did our cousin say when you left him?

'Farewell:' / And, for my heart disdained that my tongue / Should so profane the word, that taught me craft / To counterfeit oppression of such grief / That words seem'd buried in my sorrow's grave. / Marry, would the word 'farewell' have lengthen'd hours / And added years to his short banishment, / He should have had a volume of farewells; / But since it would not, he had none of me.

'Farewell.' And since my heart refused to let my tongue insult that word by saying it, it taught me the trick of pretending to be so overcome with grief that my words seemed buried in the grave of my sorrow. Honestly, if the word 'farewell' could have lengthened the hours and added years to his short exile, I would have given him a whole book of farewells. But since it couldn't, he got none from me.

He is our cousin, cousin; but 'tis doubt, / When time shall call him home from banishment, / Whether our kinsman come to see his friends. / Ourself, and Bushy, Bagot here and Green, / Observ'd his courtship to the common people, / How he did seem to dive into their hearts / With humble and familiar courtesy, / What reverence he did throw away on slaves, / Wooing poor craftsmen with the craft of smiles / And patient underbearing of his fortune, / As 'twere to banish their affects with him. / Off goes his bonnet to an oyster-wench; / A brace of draymen bid God speed him well, / And had the tribute of his supple knee, / With 'Thanks, my countrymen, my loving friends'; / As were our England in reversion his, / And he our subjects' next degree in hope.

He is our cousin, cousin. But when time calls him home from exile, it's doubtful whether our relative will come back to see his friends. I myself, and Bushy, Bagot and Green here, watched him courting the common people: how he seemed to dive into their hearts with humble, friendly politeness, how much respect he wasted on lowly people, winning over poor workmen with crafty smiles and with the patient way he bore his bad luck, as if to take their love into exile with him. Off comes his cap to an oyster-seller. A couple of cart drivers wished him God speed, and got a bow of his bending knee and 'Thank you, my countrymen, my loving friends', as if our England would be his after me, and he were next in line in my subjects' hopes.

Well, he is gone; and with him go these thoughts. / Now for the rebels which stand out in Ireland; / Expedient manage must be made, my liege, / Ere further leisure yield them further means / For their advantage and your highness' loss.

Well, he's gone, and these thoughts can go with him. Now for the rebels who are holding out in Ireland. Quick action must be taken, my lord, before any more delay gives them more chances to gain advantage and cause your Highness loss.

We will ourself in person to this war. / And, for our coffers, with too great a court / And liberal largess, are grown somewhat light, / We are enforc'd to farm our royal realm; / The revenue whereof shall furnish us / For our affairs in hand. If that come short, / Our substitutes at home shall have blank charters; / Whereto, when they shall know what men are rich, / They shall subscribe them for large sums of gold, / And send them after to supply our wants; / For we will make for Ireland presently.

I will go to this war in person. And because my treasury has got rather light from keeping too large a court and giving generous gifts, I am forced to lease out my royal kingdom for rent. The income from it will pay for the business in hand. If that is not enough, my deputies at home shall have blank documents. When they find out which men are rich, they will fill in those men's names for large sums of gold and send the money after me to supply what I need. I am leaving for Ireland at once.
Old John of Gaunt is grievous sick, my lord, / Suddenly taken, and hath sent poste-haste / To entreat your Majesty to visit him.
Old John of Gaunt is seriously ill, my lord. It came on suddenly, and he has sent in great haste to ask your Majesty to visit him.

Now put it, God, in his physician's mind / To help him to his grave immediately! / The lining of his coffers shall make coats / To deck our soldiers for these Irish wars. / Come, gentlemen, let's all go visit him: / Pray God we may make haste, and come too late!

Now, God, put it into his doctor's mind to help him into his grave at once! The lining of his money chests will make coats for our soldiers in these Irish wars. Come, gentlemen, let's all go and visit him. Pray God we hurry and arrive too late!
Will the King come, that I may breathe my last / In wholesome counsel to his unstaid youth?
Will the King come, so that I can spend my last breath giving good advice to his reckless youth?
Vex not yourself, nor strive not with your breath; / For all in vain comes counsel to his ear.
Don't upset yourself or strain your breath. Advice is wasted on his ears.

O! but they say the tongues of dying men / Enforce attention like deep harmony: / Where words are scarce, they are seldom spent in vain, / For they breathe truth that breathe their words in pain. / He that no more must say is listen'd more / Than they whom youth and ease have taught to glose; / More are men's ends mark'd than their lives before: / The setting sun, and music at the close, / As the last taste of sweets, is sweetest last, / Writ in remembrance more than things long past: / Though Richard my life's counsel would not hear, / My death's sad tale may yet undeaf his ear.

Oh, but they say the words of dying men command attention like solemn music. When words are few, they are rarely wasted, because those who speak in pain speak the truth. A man who will soon say nothing more is listened to more than those whom youth and comfort have taught to flatter. People notice how men end more than how they lived before. The setting sun, and music as it closes, like the last taste of something sweet, are sweetest at the end and stay in the memory longer than things long past. Though Richard would not listen to my advice while I lived, my sad words as I die may still unblock his ears.

No; it is stopp'd with other flattering sounds, / As praises of his state: then there are fond, / Lascivious metres, to whose venom sound / The open ear of youth doth always listen: / Report of fashions in proud Italy, / Whose manners still our tardy apish nation / Limps after in base imitation. / Where doth the world thrust forth a vanity,— / So it be new there's no respect how vile,— / That is not quickly buzz'd into his ears? / Then all too late comes counsel to be heard, / Where will doth mutiny with wit's regard. / Direct not him whose way himself will choose: / 'Tis breath thou lack'st, and that breath wilt thou lose.

No. His ears are stuffed with other, flattering sounds, like praise of his greatness. Then there are silly, lustful poems, whose poisonous sound young ears are always open to, and reports of the fashions in proud Italy, whose manners our slow, copycat nation limps after in cheap imitation. Where in the world is there a new vanity, and if it's new, nobody cares how vile it is, that isn't quickly buzzed into his ears? Advice comes much too late to be heard when desire rebels against reason. Don't try to steer someone who insists on choosing his own way. You are short of breath, and you will lose what breath you have.

Methinks I am a prophet new inspir'd, / And thus expiring do foretell of him: / His rash fierce blaze of riot cannot last, / For violent fires soon burn out themselves; / Small showers last long, but sudden storms are short; / He tires betimes that spurs too fast betimes; / With eager feeding food doth choke the feeder: / Light vanity, insatiate cormorant, / Consuming means, soon preys upon itself. / This royal throne of kings, this scepter'd isle, / This earth of majesty, this seat of Mars, / This other Eden, demi-paradise, / This fortress built by Nature for herself / Against infection and the hand of war, / This happy breed of men, this little world, / This precious stone set in the silver sea, / Which serves it in the office of a wall, / Or as a moat defensive to a house, / Against the envy of less happier lands; / This blessed plot, this earth, this realm, this England, / This nurse, this teeming womb of royal kings, / Fear'd by their breed, and famous by their birth, / Renowned for their deeds as far from home,— / For Christian service and true chivalry,— / As is the sepulchre in stubborn Jewry / Of the world's ransom, blessed Mary's Son: / This land of such dear souls, this dear, dear land, / Dear for her reputation through the world, / Is now leas'd out,—I die pronouncing it,— / Like to a tenement or pelting farm: / England, bound in with the triumphant sea, / Whose rocky shore beats back the envious siege / Of watery Neptune, is now bound in with shame, / With inky blots, and rotten parchment bonds: / That England, that was wont to conquer others, / Hath made a shameful conquest of itself. / Ah! would the scandal vanish with my life, / How happy then were my ensuing death.

I feel I am a prophet newly inspired, and as I breathe my last I predict this about him: his reckless, fierce blaze of wild living cannot last, because violent fires soon burn themselves out. Light showers last a long time, but sudden storms are short. A man who spurs his horse too fast too early soon tires. Eating too greedily chokes the eater. Empty vanity, that greedy bird that is never full, soon eats itself once it has used up everything else. This royal throne of kings, this island ruled by a sceptre, this land of majesty, this home of the god of war, this second Eden, this half-paradise, this fortress that Nature built for herself against disease and the hand of war, this happy race of men, this little world, this precious stone set in the silver sea, which acts as a wall for it, or as a defensive moat around a house, against the envy of less fortunate countries; this blessed plot of ground, this earth, this kingdom, this England, this nurse, this fertile womb of royal kings, feared because of their ancestry and famous for their birth, renowned for their deeds as far from home, in Christian service and true knighthood, as the tomb, in stubborn Judea, of the world's saviour, blessed Mary's Son; this land of such dear souls, this dear, dear land, dear for its reputation throughout the world, is now leased out, and I die as I say it, like a rented house or a miserable farm. England, surrounded by the triumphant sea, whose rocky shore beats back the jealous attacks of the sea god Neptune, is now surrounded by shame, by inky blots and rotten paper contracts. That England, which used to conquer others, has made a shameful conquest of itself. Ah, if the disgrace would vanish when I die, how happy my coming death would be!
The King is come: deal mildly with his youth; / For young hot colts, being rag'd, do rage the more.
The King has come. Go gently with his youth, because hot young horses get wilder if you enrage them.
How fares our noble uncle, Lancaster?
How is our noble uncle Lancaster?
What comfort, man? How is't with aged Gaunt?
How are you, man? How is old Gaunt?

O! how that name befits my composition; / Old Gaunt, indeed; and gaunt in being old: / Within me grief hath kept a tedious fast; / And who abstains from meat that is not gaunt? / For sleeping England long time have I watch'd; / Watching breeds leanness, leanness is all gaunt. / The pleasure that some fathers feed upon / Is my strict fast, I mean my children's looks; / And therein fasting, hast thou made me gaunt. / Gaunt am I for the grave, gaunt as a grave, / Whose hollow womb inherits nought but bones.

Oh, how well that name suits my condition! Old Gaunt indeed, and gaunt from being old. Grief has kept a long fast inside me, and who goes without food and isn't gaunt? I have kept watch over sleeping England for a long time. Staying awake makes you thin, and thinness is all gaunt. The pleasure some fathers feed on, I mean the sight of their children, I have been strictly denied. And by making me fast from that, you have made me gaunt. I am gaunt and ready for the grave, gaunt as a grave, whose hollow belly holds nothing but bones.
Can sick men play so nicely with their names?
Can sick men play so cleverly with their names?
No, misery makes sport to mock itself: / Since thou dost seek to kill my name in me, / I mock my name, great king, to flatter thee.
No, misery mocks itself for entertainment. Since you are trying to kill my name in my son, I mock my name, great King, to flatter you.
Should dying men flatter with those that live?
Should dying men flatter the living?
No, no; men living flatter those that die.
No, no; the living flatter the dying.
Thou, now a-dying, sayest thou flatterest me.
You, who are dying now, say you are flattering me.
O, no! thou diest, though I the sicker be.
Oh, no! You are the one who is dying, though I am the sicker.
I am in health, I breathe, and see thee ill.
I am healthy, I am breathing, and I see you are ill.

Now, he that made me knows I see thee ill; / Ill in myself to see, and in thee seeing ill. / Thy death-bed is no lesser than thy land / Wherein thou liest in reputation sick: / And thou, too careless patient as thou art, / Committ'st thy anointed body to the cure / Of those physicians that first wounded thee: / A thousand flatterers sit within thy crown, / Whose compass is no bigger than thy head; / And yet, incaged in so small a verge, / The waste is no whit lesser than thy land. / O! had thy grandsire, with a prophet's eye, / Seen how his son's son should destroy his sons, / From forth thy reach he would have laid thy shame, / Deposing thee before thou wert possess'd, / Which art possess'd now to depose thyself. / Why, cousin, wert thou regent of the world, / It were a shame to let this land by lease; / But for thy world enjoying but this land, / Is it not more than shame to shame it so? / Landlord of England art thou now, not king: / Thy state of law is bondslave to the law, / And—

Now, God who made me knows I see you are ill. I am ill myself, and ill to see you doing wrong. Your deathbed is nothing less than your whole country, where your reputation lies sick. And you, careless patient that you are, hand your anointed body over to be cured by the same doctors who wounded you in the first place. A thousand flatterers sit inside your crown, whose circle is no bigger than your head. And yet, though they are caged in such a small space, the damage they do is as big as your whole country. Oh, if your grandfather had seen with a prophet's eye how his son's son would destroy his sons, he would have put your shame out of your reach by deposing you before you inherited, you who are now possessed by madness to depose yourself. Why, cousin, if you ruled the whole world, it would be shameful to lease out this land. But since this land is the only world you have, isn't it worse than shameful to shame it like this? You are England's landlord now, not its king. Your legal position makes you a slave to the law, and...

And thou a lunatic lean-witted fool, / Presuming on an ague's privilege, / Dar'st with thy frozen admonition / Make pale our cheek, chasing the royal blood / With fury from his native residence. / Now by my seat's right royal majesty, / Wert thou not brother to great Edward's son,— / This tongue that runs so roundly in thy head / Should run thy head from thy unreverent shoulders.

And you, a mad, half-witted fool, taking advantage of the privilege a fever gives you, dare to make my cheeks pale with your frozen warning, chasing the royal blood from its natural home with anger. Now, by the royal majesty of my throne, if you weren't the brother of great Edward's son, this tongue that runs so freely in your head would run your head right off your disrespectful shoulders.

O! spare me not, my brother Edward's son, / For that I was his father Edward's son. / That blood already, like the pelican, / Hast thou tapp'd out, and drunkenly carous'd: / My brother Gloucester, plain well-meaning soul,— / Whom fair befall in heaven 'mongst happy souls!— / May be a precedent and witness good / That thou respect'st not spilling Edward's blood: / Join with the present sickness that I have; / And thy unkindness be like crooked age, / To crop at once a too-long withered flower. / Live in thy shame, but die not shame with thee! / These words hereafter thy tormentors be! / Convey me to my bed, then to my grave: / Love they to live that love and honour have.

Oh, don't spare me, my brother Edward's son, just because I was his father Edward's son. Like the pelican chick that feeds on its mother's blood, you have already drained that blood and drunk it greedily. My brother Gloucester, a simple, well-meaning soul (may he be happy in heaven among blessed souls!), is a good example and proof that you don't care about spilling Edward's blood. Join forces with the sickness I have now, and let your cruelty, like bent old age, cut down at once a flower that has been withered too long. Live with your shame, but don't let your shame die with you! May these words torment you from now on! Carry me to my bed, then to my grave. Let those who have love and honour wish to live.
And let them die that age and sullens have; / For both hast thou, and both become the grave.
And let those who are old and sulky die. You have both, and both are fit for the grave.
I do beseech your Majesty, impute his words / To wayward sickliness and age in him: / He loves you, on my life, and holds you dear / As Harry Duke of Hereford, were he here.
I beg your Majesty to put his words down to the bad temper of sickness and age. On my life, he loves you and holds you as dear as Harry Duke of Hereford, if he were here.
Right, you say true: as Hereford's love, so his; / As theirs, so mine; and all be as it is.
Right, you're quite right. His love is like Hereford's, and mine is like theirs. And let everything be as it is.
My liege, old Gaunt commends him to your Majesty.
My lord, old Gaunt sends his respects to your Majesty.
Nay, nothing; all is said: / His tongue is now a stringless instrument; / Words, life, and all, old Lancaster hath spent.
No, nothing. Everything is said. His tongue is now an instrument without strings. Old Lancaster has used up his words, his life, everything.
Be York the next that must be bankrupt so! / Though death be poor, it ends a mortal woe.
May York be the next to go bankrupt like that! Death may be poor, but it ends human misery.

The ripest fruit first falls, and so doth he: / His time is spent; our pilgrimage must be. / So much for that. Now for our Irish wars. / We must supplant those rough rug-headed kerns, / Which live like venom where no venom else / But only they have privilege to live. / And for these great affairs do ask some charge, / Towards our assistance we do seize to us / The plate, coin, revenues, and moveables, / Whereof our uncle Gaunt did stand possess'd.

The ripest fruit falls first, and so does he. His time is over; our journey through life must go on. So much for that. Now for our Irish wars. We must get rid of those rough, shaggy-haired Irish foot soldiers, who live like poison in a country where nothing else poisonous is allowed to live. And because these great matters cost money, to help pay for them I take for myself the silver plate, coins, income and possessions that belonged to our uncle Gaunt.

How long shall I be patient? Ah! how long / Shall tender duty make me suffer wrong? / Not Gloucester's death, nor Hereford's banishment, / Nor Gaunt's rebukes, nor England's private wrongs, / Nor the prevention of poor Bolingbroke / About his marriage, nor my own disgrace, / Have ever made me sour my patient cheek, / Or bend one wrinkle on my sovereign's face. / I am the last of noble Edward's sons, / Of whom thy father, Prince of Wales, was first; / In war was never lion rag'd more fierce, / In peace was never gentle lamb more mild, / Than was that young and princely gentleman. / His face thou hast, for even so look'd he, / Accomplish'd with the number of thy hours; / But when he frown'd, it was against the French, / And not against his friends; his noble hand / Did win what he did spend, and spent not that / Which his triumphant father's hand had won: / His hands were guilty of no kindred's blood, / But bloody with the enemies of his kin. / O Richard! York is too far gone with grief, / Or else he never would compare between.

How long shall I be patient? Ah, how long will my gentle sense of duty make me put up with wrong? Not Gloucester's death, not Hereford's exile, not Gaunt's humiliations, not England's private wrongs, not the way poor Bolingbroke's marriage abroad was blocked, not my own disgrace, has ever made me sour my patient face or frown even once at my king. I am the last of noble Edward's sons, of whom your father, the Prince of Wales, was the eldest. In war no lion ever raged more fiercely, and in peace no gentle lamb was ever milder, than that young prince. You have his face; he looked just like you when he was your age. But when he frowned, it was against the French, not against his friends. His noble hand won what he spent, and did not spend what his victorious father's hand had won. His hands were guilty of no relative's blood, but bloody with the blood of his family's enemies. Oh, Richard! York is too overcome with grief, or he would never make this comparison.

O! my liege. / Pardon me, if you please; if not, I, pleas'd / Not to be pardon'd, am content withal. / Seek you to seize and gripe into your hands / The royalties and rights of banish'd Hereford? / Is not Gaunt dead, and doth not Hereford live? / Was not Gaunt just, and is not Harry true? / Did not the one deserve to have an heir? / Is not his heir a well-deserving son? / Take Hereford's rights away, and take from Time / His charters and his customary rights; / Let not to-morrow then ensue to-day; / Be not thyself; for how art thou a king / But by fair sequence and succession? / Now, afore God,—God forbid I say true!— / If you do wrongfully seize Hereford's rights, / Call in the letters-patents that he hath / By his attorneys-general to sue / His livery, and deny his offer'd homage, / You pluck a thousand dangers on your head, / You lose a thousand well-disposed hearts, / And prick my tender patience to those thoughts / Which honour and allegiance cannot think.

Oh, my lord, forgive me if you want to. If not, I'm happy not to be forgiven. Are you trying to seize and grab into your hands the royal grants and rights of banished Hereford? Isn't Gaunt dead, and isn't Hereford alive? Wasn't Gaunt honourable, and isn't Harry loyal? Didn't the one deserve to have an heir? Isn't his heir a deserving son? Take away Hereford's rights, and you take away Time's legal charters and customary rights. Then don't let tomorrow follow today. Don't be yourself; for how are you a king except by proper order and succession? Now, before God, and God forbid I'm right, if you wrongfully seize Hereford's rights, cancel the royal letters that allow his lawyers to claim his inheritance, and refuse his offer of loyalty, you will pull a thousand dangers down on your head, lose a thousand well-meaning hearts, and push my gentle patience towards thoughts that a man of honour and loyalty cannot think.
Think what you will: we seize into our hands / His plate, his goods, his money, and his lands.
Think what you like. I am taking his silver, his goods, his money and his lands into my hands.
I'll not be by the while: my liege, farewell: / What will ensue hereof there's none can tell; / But by bad courses may be understood / That their events can never fall out good.
I won't be here while that happens. My lord, goodbye. No one can tell what will come of this; but we can understand from bad actions that their results can never turn out well.

Go, Bushy, to the Earl of Wiltshire straight: / Bid him repair to us to Ely House / To see this business. To-morrow next / We will for Ireland; and 'tis time, I trow: / And we create, in absence of ourself, / Our Uncle York lord governor of England; / For he is just, and always lov'd us well. / Come on, our queen: to-morrow must we part; / Be merry, for our time of stay is short.

Bushy, go to the Earl of Wiltshire at once. Tell him to come to me at Ely House to deal with this business. Tomorrow I leave for Ireland, and it's high time, I think. While I am away I make my uncle York governor of England, because he is fair and has always loved me. Come on, my queen. Tomorrow we must part. Be cheerful, because our time together is short.
Well, lords, the Duke of Lancaster is dead.
Well, lords, the Duke of Lancaster is dead.
And living too; for now his son is Duke.
And alive too, because now his son is Duke.
Barely in title, not in revenues.
Only in title, not in income.
Richly in both, if justice had her right.
Rich in both, if justice had its way.
My heart is great; but it must break with silence, / Ere't be disburdened with a liberal tongue.
My heart is full, but it must break in silence before I relieve it by speaking freely.
Nay, speak thy mind; and let him ne'er speak more / That speaks thy words again to do thee harm!
No, say what you think, and may anyone who repeats your words to harm you never speak again!
Tends that thou wouldst speak to the Duke of Hereford? / If it be so, out with it boldly, man; / Quick is mine ear to hear of good towards him.
Is what you want to say about the Duke of Hereford? If so, out with it boldly, man. My ears are quick to hear good news about him.
No good at all that I can do for him, / Unless you call it good to pity him, / Bereft and gelded of his patrimony.
There's no good I can do for him, unless you call it good to pity him, robbed and stripped of his inheritance.

Now, afore God, 'tis shame such wrongs are borne / In him, a royal prince, and many moe / Of noble blood in this declining land. / The king is not himself, but basely led / By flatterers; and what they will inform, / Merely in hate, 'gainst any of us all, / That will the king severely prosecute / 'Gainst us, our lives, our children, and our heirs.

Now, before God, it's shameful that such wrongs are done to him, a royal prince, and to many others of noble blood in this declining country. The king is not himself, but is shamefully led by flatterers; and whatever they tell him out of pure hatred against any of us, the king will harshly punish us for it, our lives, our children and our heirs.
The commons hath he pill'd with grievous taxes, / And quite lost their hearts: the nobles hath he fin'd / For ancient quarrels and quite lost their hearts.
He has stripped the common people with heavy taxes and lost their hearts completely. He has fined the nobles for old quarrels and lost their hearts completely too.
And daily new exactions are devis'd; / As blanks, benevolences, and I wot not what: / But what, o' God's name, doth become of this?
And every day new ways of squeezing money are invented, like blank charters, forced 'gifts' and who knows what. But what, in God's name, happens to all this money?
Wars hath not wasted it, for warr'd he hath not, / But basely yielded upon compromise / That which his ancestors achiev'd with blows. / More hath he spent in peace than they in wars.
Wars haven't used it up, because he hasn't fought any. Instead he has shamefully given up, by making deals, what his ancestors won with blows. He has spent more in peace than they did in war.
The Earl of Wiltshire hath the realm in farm.
The Earl of Wiltshire has the kingdom on lease.
The King's grown bankrupt like a broken man.
The King has gone bankrupt like a ruined man.
Reproach and dissolution hangeth over him.
Disgrace and ruin are hanging over him.
