He hath not money for these Irish wars, / His burdenous taxations notwithstanding, / But by the robbing of the banish'd Duke.
In spite of his heavy taxes, he has no money for these Irish wars except by robbing the banished Duke.

His noble kinsman: most degenerate king! / But, lords, we hear this fearful tempest sing, / Yet seek no shelter to avoid the storm; / We see the wind sit sore upon our sails, / And yet we strike not, but securely perish.

His own noble relative. What a degenerate king! But, lords, we hear this terrible storm howling, and yet we look for no shelter from it. We see the wind pressing hard on our sails, and yet we don't lower them, but carelessly go to our deaths.
We see the very wrack that we must suffer; / And unavoided is the danger now, / For suffering so the causes of our wrack.
We can see the very shipwreck we are going to suffer, and the danger can't be avoided now, because we have put up with the causes of our wreck for so long.
Not so: even through the hollow eyes of death / I spy life peering; but I dare not say / How near the tidings of our comfort is.
Not so. Even through the hollow eyes of death's skull I can see life peeping out; but I don't dare say how close the news of our rescue is.
Nay, let us share thy thoughts as thou dost ours.
No, share your thoughts with us, as you share ours.
Be confident to speak, Northumberland: / We three are but thyself: and, speaking so, / Thy words are but as thoughts; therefore be bold.
Speak with confidence, Northumberland. We three are the same as you, and so, said to us, your words are no more than thoughts. So be bold.

Then thus: I have from Le Port Blanc, a bay / In Brittany, receiv'd intelligence / That Harry Duke of Hereford, Rainold Lord Cobham, / That late broke from the Duke of Exeter, / His brother, Archbishop late of Canterbury, / Sir Thomas Erpingham, Sir John Ramston, / Sir John Norbery, Sir Robert Waterton, and Francis Quoint, / All these well furnish'd by the Duke of Britaine, / With eight tall ships, three thousand men of war, / Are making hither with all due expedience, / And shortly mean to touch our northern shore. / Perhaps they had ere this, but that they stay / The first departing of the king for Ireland. / If then we shall shake off our slavish yoke, / Imp out our drooping country's broken wing, / Redeem from broking pawn the blemish'd crown, / Wipe off the dust that hides our sceptre's gilt, / And make high majesty look like itself, / Away with me in post to Ravenspurgh; / But if you faint, as fearing to do so, / Stay and be secret, and myself will go.

Then here it is. I have had news from Port Blanc, a bay in Brittany, that Harry Duke of Hereford, Rainold Lord Cobham, the son of the Earl of Arundel who recently escaped from the Duke of Exeter, his brother the former Archbishop of Canterbury, Sir Thomas Erpingham, Sir John Ramston, Sir John Norbery, Sir Robert Waterton and Francis Quoint, all well equipped by the Duke of Brittany with eight large ships and three thousand soldiers, are heading here as fast as they can and plan to land on our northern coast soon. Perhaps they would have landed already, but they are waiting for the king to leave for Ireland first. So if we are going to throw off our slavery, repair our drooping country's broken wing, buy back the stained crown from the pawnbroker, wipe off the dust that hides the gold of our sceptre and make royal majesty look like itself again, come with me at full speed to Ravenspurgh. But if you lose your nerve and are afraid to, stay here and keep it secret, and I will go myself.
To horse, to horse! Urge doubts to them that fear.
To horse, to horse! Raise your doubts with those who are afraid.
Hold out my horse, and I will first be there.
If my horse holds out, I'll be there first.
Madam, your Majesty is too much sad. / You promis'd, when you parted with the king, / To lay aside life-harming heaviness, / And entertain a cheerful disposition.
Madam, your Majesty is much too sad. When you said goodbye to the king, you promised to put aside this sadness that harms your health and to keep cheerful.

To please the King, I did; to please myself / I cannot do it; yet I know no cause / Why I should welcome such a guest as grief, / Save bidding farewell to so sweet a guest / As my sweet Richard: yet again methinks, / Some unborn sorrow, ripe in fortune's womb, / Is coming towards me, and my inward soul / With nothing trembles; at some thing it grieves / More than with parting from my lord the king.

I promised to please the King. To please myself I cannot do it. And yet I know no reason why I should welcome such a guest as grief, except that I have said goodbye to such a sweet guest as my sweet Richard. And yet I feel that some sorrow not yet born, ripe in the womb of fortune, is coming towards me, and my inner soul trembles at nothing. It grieves at something more than parting from my husband the king.

Each substance of a grief hath twenty shadows, / Which shows like grief itself, but is not so; / For sorrow's eye, glazed with blinding tears, / Divides one thing entire to many objects; / Like perspectives which, rightly gaz'd upon, / Show nothing but confusion; ey'd awry, / Distinguish form: so your sweet Majesty, / Looking awry upon your lord's departure, / Find shapes of grief more than himself to wail; / Which, look'd on as it is, is nought but shadows / Of what it is not. Then, thrice-gracious Queen, / More than your lord's departure weep not: more's not seen; / Or if it be, 'tis with false sorrow's eye, / Which for things true weeps things imaginary.

Every real grief casts twenty shadows that look like grief itself but are not. Sorrow's eye, glazed with blinding tears, splits one whole thing into many, like those trick pictures which show nothing but a blur when you look at them straight on, but show a clear shape when you look at them from the side. In the same way, your sweet Majesty, looking at your husband's departure from the wrong angle, finds more shapes of grief in it than the departure itself; and those, seen as they really are, are only shadows of what is not there. So, most gracious Queen, weep for nothing more than your husband's departure. There is nothing more to see; or if there is, it is seen with sorrow's false eye, which weeps for imaginary things as if they were real.

It may be so; but yet my inward soul / Persuades me it is otherwise: howe'er it be, / I cannot but be sad, so heavy sad / As, though in thinking, on no thought I think, / Makes me with heavy nothing faint and shrink.
That may be so; but my inner soul tells me it's otherwise. However it is, I can't help being sad, so heavily sad that, though I try to think of nothing, this heavy nothing makes me faint and shrink.
'Tis nothing but conceit, my gracious lady.
It's nothing but imagination, my gracious lady.

'Tis nothing less: conceit is still deriv'd / From some forefather grief; mine is not so, / For nothing hath begot my something grief, / Or something hath the nothing that I grieve: / 'Tis in reversion that I do possess; / But what it is, that is not yet known; what / I cannot name; 'tis nameless woe, I wot.

It's anything but that. Imagination always comes from some earlier grief. Mine isn't like that, because nothing has given birth to my something grief, or else something has the nothing I grieve about. It's as if I own a grief that is still to come to me; but what it is, I don't yet know. I can't name it. It's a nameless sorrow, I'm sure.
God save your majesty! and well met, gentlemen: / I hope the King is not yet shipp'd for Ireland.
God save your majesty! And good to see you, gentlemen. I hope the King hasn't sailed for Ireland yet.
Why hop'st thou so? 'Tis better hope he is, / For his designs crave haste, his haste good hope: / Then wherefore dost thou hope he is not shipp'd?
Why do you hope that? It's better to hope he has, because his plans need speed, and his speed gives us good hope. So why do you hope he hasn't sailed?

That he, our hope, might have retir'd his power, / And driven into despair an enemy's hope / Who strongly hath set footing in this land: / The banish'd Bolingbroke repeals himself, / And with uplifted arms is safe arriv'd / At Ravenspurgh.

So that he, our hope, could have brought his army back and driven to despair the hopes of an enemy who has landed in force in this country. The banished Bolingbroke has called himself back from exile, and has arrived safely at Ravenspurgh with his weapons raised.
Ah! madam, 'tis too true; and that is worse, / The Lord Northumberland, his son young Henry Percy, / The Lords of Ross, Beaumond, and Willoughby, / With all their powerful friends, are fled to him.
Ah, madam, it's all too true. And what is worse, Lord Northumberland, his son young Henry Percy, the Lords of Ross, Beaumond and Willoughby, with all their powerful friends, have gone over to him.
Why have you not proclaim'd Northumberland / And all the rest revolted faction traitors?
Why haven't you declared Northumberland and all the rest of the rebel group traitors?
We have: whereupon the Earl of Worcester / Hath broken his staff, resign'd his stewardship, / And all the household servants fled with him / To Bolingbroke.
We have. And so the Earl of Worcester has broken his staff of office, resigned as steward, and all the servants of the royal household have run off with him to Bolingbroke.

So, Green, thou art the midwife to my woe, / And Bolingbroke my sorrow's dismal heir: / Now hath my soul brought forth her prodigy, / And I, a gasping new-deliver'd mother, / Have woe to woe, sorrow to sorrow join'd.

So, Green, you are the midwife of my sorrow, and Bolingbroke is the dreadful child of my sadness. Now my soul has given birth to its monster, and I, a gasping mother who has just delivered, have joined sorrow to sorrow and grief to grief.

Who shall hinder me? / I will despair, and be at enmity / With cozening hope: he is a flatterer, / A parasite, a keeper-back of death, / Who gently would dissolve the bands of life, / Which false hope lingers in extremity.

Who will stop me? I will despair and be the enemy of cheating hope. Hope is a flatterer, a hanger-on, something that holds back death, which would gently untie the bonds of life that false hope keeps dragging out at the very end.
Here comes the Duke of York.
Here comes the Duke of York.
With signs of war about his aged neck: / O! full of careful business are his looks. / Uncle, for God's sake, speak comfortable words.
With armour round his old neck. Oh, his face is full of worried business! Uncle, for God's sake, say something comforting.

Should I do so, I should belie my thoughts: / Comfort's in heaven; and we are on the earth, / Where nothing lives but crosses, cares, and grief. / Your husband, he is gone to save far off, / Whilst others come to make him lose at home. / Here am I left to underprop his land, / Who, weak with age, cannot support myself. / Now comes the sick hour that his surfeit made; / Now shall he try his friends that flatter'd him.

If I did, I would be lying about my thoughts. Comfort is in heaven, and we are on earth, where there is nothing but trouble, worry and grief. Your husband has gone far away to save one land, while others come to make him lose this one at home. I am left here to prop up his country, when I am so weak with age I can't support myself. Now comes the sickness that his excesses have caused. Now he will find out what his flattering friends are worth.
My lord, your son was gone before I came.
My lord, your son had gone before I got there.

He was? Why, so! go all which way it will! / The nobles they are fled, the commons they are cold, / And will, I fear, revolt on Hereford's side. / Sirrah, get thee to Plashy, to my sister Gloucester; / Bid her send me presently a thousand pound. / Hold, take my ring.

He had? Well then, let everything go whichever way it likes! The nobles have run away, the common people are unenthusiastic and, I fear, will rebel on Hereford's side. You, go to Plashy, to my sister-in-law Gloucester. Tell her to send me a thousand pounds at once. Wait, take my ring.
My lord, I had forgot to tell your lordship: / To-day, as I came by, I called there; / But I shall grieve you to report the rest.
My lord, I forgot to tell your lordship. Today I called there on my way here; but it will upset you to hear the rest.
An hour before I came the duchess died.
An hour before I arrived, the duchess died.

God for his mercy! what a tide of woes / Comes rushing on this woeful land at once! / I know not what to do: I would to God,— / So my untruth had not provok'd him to it,— / The king had cut off my head with my brother's. / What! are there no posts dispatch'd for Ireland? / How shall we do for money for these wars? / Come, sister,—cousin, I would say,—pray, pardon me.— / Go, fellow, get thee home; provide some carts, / And bring away the armour that is there.

God have mercy! What a flood of sorrows comes rushing over this sad country all at once! I don't know what to do. I wish to God, as long as it wasn't disloyalty in me that provoked him, that the king had cut off my head along with my brother's. What! Haven't any messengers been sent to Ireland? How will we find money for these wars? Come, sister... cousin, I mean. Please forgive me. Go, man, go home, get some carts and bring away the armour that's there.

Gentlemen, will you go muster men? / If I know how or which way to order these affairs / Thus disorderly thrust into my hands, / Never believe me. Both are my kinsmen: / T'one is my sovereign, whom both my oath / And duty bids defend; the other again / Is my kinsman, whom the king hath wrong'd, / Whom conscience and my kindred bids to right. / Well, somewhat we must do. Come, cousin, / I'll dispose of you. Gentlemen, go muster up your men, / And meet me presently at Berkeley Castle. / I should to Plashy too: / But time will not permit. All is uneven, / And everything is left at six and seven.

Gentlemen, will you go and gather troops? If I know how or which way to manage these affairs that have been shoved into my hands in such a mess, never believe me again. Both are my relatives. One is my king, whom my oath and my duty both tell me to defend. The other is also my relative, whom the king has wronged, and whom my conscience and family feeling tell me to put right. Well, we must do something. Come, cousin, I'll find a place for you. Gentlemen, go and gather your men and meet me straight away at Berkeley Castle. I ought to go to Plashy too, but there isn't time. Everything is uneven, and everything is in total confusion.
The wind sits fair for news to go to Ireland, / But none returns. For us to levy power / Proportionable to the enemy / Is all unpossible.
The wind is good for sending news to Ireland, but no news comes back. For us to raise an army as big as the enemy's is completely impossible.
Besides, our nearness to the king in love / Is near the hate of those love not the king.
Besides, the King's love for us makes us close to the hatred of those who don't love the king.
And that is the wavering commons; for their love / Lies in their purses; and whoso empties them, / By so much fills their hearts with deadly hate.
And that means the unreliable common people, because their love lies in their purses, and whoever empties them fills their hearts with deadly hatred just as much.
Wherein the king stands generally condemn'd.
And that's why the king is hated by almost everyone.
If judgment lie in them, then so do we, / Because we ever have been near the king.
If they are to be the judges, then so are we condemned, because we have always been close to the king.
Well, I will for refuge straight to Bristol Castle. / The Earl of Wiltshire is already there.
Well, I'm going straight to Bristol Castle for safety. The Earl of Wiltshire is already there.
Thither will I with you; for little office / Will the hateful commons perform for us, / Except like curs to tear us all to pieces. / Will you go along with us?
I'll go there with you, because the hateful common people won't do much for us except tear us all to pieces like dogs. Will you come with us?
No; I will to Ireland to his Majesty. / Farewell: If heart's presages be not vain, / We three here part that ne'er shall meet again.
No. I will go to Ireland to his Majesty. Goodbye. If my heart's forebodings are right, we three are parting here and will never meet again.
That's as York thrives to beat back Bolingbroke.
That depends on whether York succeeds in beating back Bolingbroke.
Alas, poor Duke! the task he undertakes / Is numb'ring sands and drinking oceans dry: / Where one on his side fights, thousands will fly. / Farewell at once; for once, for all, and ever.

Alas, poor Duke! The task he is taking on is like counting the sands and drinking the oceans dry. For every one who fights on his side, thousands will run away. Goodbye now, once and for all, and for ever.
How far is it, my lord, to Berkeley now?
How far is it to Berkeley now, my lord?

Believe me, noble lord, / I am a stranger here in Gloucestershire. / These high wild hills and rough uneven ways / Draws out our miles, and makes them wearisome; / And yet your fair discourse hath been as sugar, / Making the hard way sweet and delectable. / But I bethink me what a weary way / From Ravenspurgh to Cotswold will be found / In Ross and Willoughby, wanting your company, / Which, I protest, hath very much beguil'd / The tediousness and process of my travel. / But theirs is sweeten'd with the hope to have / The present benefit which I possess; / And hope to joy is little less in joy / Than hope enjoy'd: by this the weary lords / Shall make their way seem short, as mine hath done / By sight of what I have, your noble company.

Believe me, noble lord, I don't know my way around Gloucestershire. These high, wild hills and rough, bumpy roads stretch out our miles and make them tiring. And yet your pleasant conversation has been like sugar, making the hard road sweet and delightful. But I think what a weary road Ross and Willoughby will find it from Ravenspurgh to the Cotswolds without your company, which, I swear, has made the dullness and length of my journey pass much more quickly. But their journey is sweetened by the hope of having the benefit I have now; and hoping for joy is not much less joyful than joy itself. In this way the weary lords will make their road seem short, as mine has been made short by having what I have: your noble company.
Of much less value is my company / Than your good words. But who comes here?
My company is worth much less than your kind words. But who is this?
It is my son, young Harry Percy, / Sent from my brother Worcester, whencesoever. / Harry, how fares your uncle?
It's my son, young Harry Percy, sent from my brother Worcester, wherever he is. Harry, how is your uncle?
I had thought, my lord, to have learn'd his health of you.
I thought I would find out how he is from you, my lord.
Why, is he not with the Queen?
Why, isn't he with the Queen?
No, my good lord; he hath forsook the court, / Broken his staff of office, and dispers'd / The household of the King.
No, my good lord. He has left the court, broken his staff of office and dismissed the King's household.
What was his reason? / He was not so resolv'd when last we spake together.
Why did he do that? He hadn't decided to when we last spoke.

Because your lordship was proclaimed traitor. / But he, my lord, is gone to Ravenspurgh, / To offer service to the Duke of Hereford; / And sent me over by Berkeley, to discover / What power the Duke of York had levied there; / Then with directions to repair to Ravenspurgh.

Because your lordship was declared a traitor. But he has gone to Ravenspurgh, my lord, to offer his service to the Duke of Hereford. He sent me by way of Berkeley to find out how many troops the Duke of York had raised there, with orders to come on to Ravenspurgh afterwards.
Have you forgot the Duke of Hereford, boy?
Have you forgotten the Duke of Hereford, boy?
No, my good lord; for that is not forgot / Which ne'er I did remember; to my knowledge, / I never in my life did look on him.
No, my good lord, because you can't forget what you never remembered. As far as I know, I have never set eyes on him in my life.
Then learn to know him now; this is the duke.
Then get to know him now. This is the duke.
My gracious lord, I tender you my service, / Such as it is, being tender, raw, and young, / Which elder days shall ripen, and confirm / To more approved service and desert.
My gracious lord, I offer you my service, such as it is, young, raw and untried. Older age will ripen it and strengthen it into more proven service and greater worth.

I thank thee, gentle Percy; and be sure / I count myself in nothing else so happy / As in a soul remembering my good friends; / And as my fortune ripens with thy love, / It shall be still thy true love's recompense. / My heart this covenant makes, my hand thus seals it.

Thank you, noble Percy. And be sure that nothing makes me happier than having a soul that remembers my good friends. As my fortune ripens with your love, it will always reward your true love. My heart makes this promise, and my hand seals it like this.
How far is it to Berkeley? And what stir / Keeps good old York there with his men of war?
How far is it to Berkeley? And what forces is good old York keeping there with his soldiers?
There stands the castle, by yon tuft of trees, / Mann'd with three hundred men, as I have heard; / And in it are the Lords of York, Berkeley, and Seymour; / None else of name and noble estimate.
There's the castle, by that clump of trees, defended by three hundred men, as I've heard. Inside are the Lords York, Berkeley and Seymour, and nobody else of high rank and importance.
Here come the Lords of Ross and Willoughby, / Bloody with spurring, fiery-red with haste.
Here come the Lords Ross and Willoughby, bloody from spurring their horses and red-faced with haste.
Welcome, my lords. I wot your love pursues / A banish'd traitor; all my treasury / Is yet but unfelt thanks, which, more enrich'd, / Shall be your love and labour's recompense.
Welcome, my lords. I know your love follows a banished traitor. All the treasure I have yet is thanks you can't touch; but when I am richer, it will reward your love and your efforts.
Your presence makes us rich, most noble lord.
Your presence makes us rich, most noble lord.
And far surmounts our labour to attain it.
And far outweighs the effort we made to reach it.
Evermore thanks, the exchequer of the poor; / Which, till my infant fortune comes to years, / Stands for my bounty. But who comes here?
Thanks again and always, the only treasury of the poor. Until my infant fortune grows up, thanks must stand for my generosity. But who is this?
It is my Lord of Berkeley, as I guess.
It's my Lord Berkeley, I think.
My Lord of Hereford, my message is to you.
My Lord of Hereford, I have a message for you.
My lord, my answer is—to Lancaster; / And I am come to seek that name in England; / And I must find that title in your tongue / Before I make reply to aught you say.
My lord, I answer only to the name Lancaster. I have come to look for that name in England, and I must hear that title from your tongue before I reply to anything you say.

Mistake me not, my lord; 'tis not my meaning / To raze one title of your honour out: / To you, my lord, I come, what lord you will, / From the most gracious regent of this land, / The Duke of York, to know what pricks you on / To take advantage of the absent time, / And fright our native peace with self-borne arms.

Don't misunderstand me, my lord. I don't mean to scratch out one title of your honour. I come to you, my lord, whatever lord you like, from the most gracious regent of this country, the Duke of York, to find out what drives you to take advantage of the King's absence and frighten our peaceful country with weapons you carry on your own authority.
I shall not need transport my words by you; / Here comes his Grace in person. / My noble uncle!
I won't need you to carry my words; here comes his Grace in person. My noble uncle!
Show me thy humble heart, and not thy knee, / Whose duty is deceivable and false.
Show me a humble heart, not a bent knee, whose show of duty is deceptive and false.

Tut, tut! / Grace me no grace, nor uncle me no uncle: / I am no traitor's uncle; and that word 'grace' / In an ungracious mouth is but profane. / Why have those banish'd and forbidden legs / Dar'd once to touch a dust of England's ground? / But then more 'why?' why have they dar'd to march / So many miles upon her peaceful bosom, / Frighting her pale-fac'd villages with war / And ostentation of despised arms? / Com'st thou because the anointed king is hence? / Why, foolish boy, the king is left behind, / And in my loyal bosom lies his power. / Were I but now lord of such hot youth / As when brave Gaunt, thy father, and myself / Rescued the Black Prince, that young Mars of men, / From forth the ranks of many thousand French, / O! then how quickly should this arm of mine, / Now prisoner to the palsy, chastise thee / And minister correction to thy fault!

Tut, tut! Don't 'grace' me, and don't 'uncle' me. I am no traitor's uncle, and that word 'grace' is an insult to God in a mouth without grace. Why have those banished, forbidden legs dared to touch even one speck of English dust? And more 'why': why have they dared to march so many miles over her peaceful breast, frightening her pale-faced villages with war and a display of hateful weapons? Have you come because the anointed king is away? Why, foolish boy, the king is left behind here, and his power lies in my loyal heart. If I were now as young and hot-blooded as when brave Gaunt, your father, and I rescued the Black Prince, that young god of war among men, from the ranks of many thousand Frenchmen, oh, how quickly this arm of mine, now trembling with palsy, would punish you and correct your fault!
My gracious uncle, let me know my fault: / On what condition stands it and wherein?
My gracious uncle, tell me what my fault is. What kind of fault is it, and where does it lie?

Even in condition of the worst degree, / In gross rebellion and detested treason: / Thou art a banish'd man, and here art come / Before the expiration of thy time, / In braving arms against thy sovereign.
It is a fault of the very worst kind: open rebellion and hateful treason. You are a banished man, and you have come here before the end of your sentence, defying your king with weapons.

As I was banish'd, I was banish'd Hereford; / But as I come, I come for Lancaster. / And, noble uncle, I beseech your Grace / Look on my wrongs with an indifferent eye: / You are my father, for methinks in you / I see old Gaunt alive: O! then, my father, / Will you permit that I shall stand condemn'd / A wandering vagabond; my rights and royalties / Pluck'd from my arms perforce, and given away / To upstart unthrifts? Wherefore was I born? / If that my cousin king be King in England, / It must be granted I am Duke of Lancaster. / You have a son, Aumerle, my noble cousin; / Had you first died, and he been thus trod down, / He should have found his uncle Gaunt a father / To rouse his wrongs and chase them to the bay. / I am denied to sue my livery here, / And yet my letters-patents give me leave. / My father's goods are all distrain'd and sold; / And these and all are all amiss employ'd. / What would you have me do? I am a subject, / And challenge law: attorneys are denied me; / And therefore personally I lay my claim / To my inheritance of free descent.

When I was banished, it was Hereford who was banished; but I come back as Lancaster. And, noble uncle, I beg your Grace to look at the wrongs done to me with an impartial eye. You are my father, because I think I see old Gaunt alive in you. Oh, then, my father, will you let me be condemned to be a wandering beggar, my rights and titles snatched from my arms by force and given away to upstart spendthrifts? What was I born for? If my cousin is King of England, it must follow that I am Duke of Lancaster. You have a son, Aumerle, my noble cousin. If you had died first and he had been trampled on like this, he would have found a father in his uncle Gaunt, to rouse up his wrongs and hunt them down. I am not allowed to claim my inheritance here, even though my royal letters give me the right. My father's goods have all been seized and sold, and all of it has been wrongly used. What do you want me to do? I am a subject and I appeal to the law. I am refused lawyers, and so I am claiming my lawful inheritance in person.
The noble Duke hath been too much abus'd.
The noble Duke has been very badly treated.
It stands your Grace upon to do him right.
Your Grace has a duty to see that he gets justice.
Base men by his endowments are made great.
Worthless men have been made great with his property.

My lords of England, let me tell you this: / I have had feeling of my cousin's wrongs, / And labour'd all I could to do him right; / But in this kind to come, in braving arms, / Be his own carver and cut out his way, / To find out right with wrong, it may not be; / And you that do abet him in this kind / Cherish rebellion, and are rebels all.

My lords of England, let me tell you this. I have felt for my nephew's wrongs and worked as hard as I could to put them right. But to come like this, in defiant arms, carving out his own way and looking for right by doing wrong, cannot be allowed. And you who help him like this are encouraging rebellion, and you are all rebels.
The noble Duke hath sworn his coming is / But for his own; and for the right of that / We all have strongly sworn to give him aid; / And let him never see joy that breaks that oath!
The noble Duke has sworn that he has come only for what is his own; and we have all solemnly sworn to help him get his rights. May anyone who breaks that oath never know joy!

Well, well, I see the issue of these arms: / I cannot mend it, I must needs confess, / Because my power is weak and all ill left; / But if I could, by him that gave me life, / I would attach you all and make you stoop / Unto the sovereign mercy of the king; / But since I cannot, be it known unto you / I do remain as neuter. So, fare you well; / Unless you please to enter in the castle, / And there repose you for this night.

Well, well, I see how this armed rising will end. I must admit I can't stop it, because my army is weak and has been badly left. But if I could, by God who gave me life, I would arrest you all and make you bow to the royal mercy of the king. But since I can't, I tell you that I will stay neutral. So, goodbye, unless you would like to come into the castle and rest there for the night.

An offer, uncle, that we will accept: / But we must win your Grace to go with us / To Bristol Castle, which they say is held / By Bushy, Bagot, and their complices, / The caterpillars of the commonwealth, / Which I have sworn to weed and pluck away.

An offer, uncle, that we accept. But we must persuade your Grace to go with us to Bristol Castle, which they say is held by Bushy, Bagot and their accomplices, the caterpillars eating up the country, which I have sworn to weed out and pull up.
It may be I will go with you; but yet I'll pause, / For I am loath to break our country's laws. / Nor friends nor foes, to me welcome you are. / Things past redress are now with me past care.

I may go with you; but I'll think about it first, because I don't want to break our country's laws. You are welcome to me neither as friends nor as enemies. Things that can't be put right are now past my worrying about.
My Lord of Salisbury, we have stay'd ten days / And hardly kept our countrymen together, / And yet we hear no tidings from the King; / Therefore we will disperse ourselves: farewell.
My Lord Salisbury, we have waited ten days and only just kept our men together, and still we hear no news from the King. So we will break up and go home. Goodbye.
Stay yet another day, thou trusty Welshman; / The King reposeth all his confidence in thee.
Stay one more day, trusty Welshman. The King puts all his trust in you.

'Tis thought the king is dead; we will not stay. / The bay trees in our country are all wither'd, / And meteors fright the fixed stars of heaven; / The pale-fac'd moon looks bloody on the earth / And lean-look'd prophets whisper fearful change; / Rich men look sad, and ruffians dance and leap, / The one in fear to lose what they enjoy, / The other to enjoy by rage and war. / These signs forerun the death or fall of kings. / Farewell: our countrymen are gone and fled, / As well assur'd Richard their king is dead.

People think the king is dead. We won't stay. The bay trees in our country have all withered, and comets frighten the fixed stars in heaven. The pale moon looks blood-red on the earth, and thin-faced prophets whisper about terrifying changes. Rich men look sad, and thugs dance and jump about, the rich because they are afraid of losing what they have, the thugs because they hope to gain from violence and war. These signs come before the death or fall of kings. Goodbye. Our countrymen have gone and run off, sure that Richard their king is dead.

Ah, Richard! with the eyes of heavy mind, / I see thy glory like a shooting star / Fall to the base earth from the firmament. / The sun sets weeping in the lowly west, / Witnessing storms to come, woe, and unrest. / Thy friends are fled, to wait upon thy foes, / And crossly to thy good all fortune goes.

Ah, Richard! With the eyes of a heavy heart I see your glory fall like a shooting star from the sky to the lowly earth. Your sun sets weeping in the humble west, foretelling storms, sorrow and trouble to come. Your friends have run off to serve your enemies, and all fortune goes against you.

Bring forth these men. / Bushy and Green, I will not vex your souls— / Since presently your souls must part your bodies— / With too much urging your pernicious lives, / For 'twere no charity; yet, to wash your blood / From off my hands, here in the view of men / I will unfold some causes of your deaths. / You have misled a prince, a royal king, / A happy gentleman in blood and lineaments, / By you unhappied and disfigur'd clean; / You have in manner with your sinful hours / Made a divorce betwixt his queen and him, / Broke the possession of a royal bed, / And stain'd the beauty of a fair queen's cheeks / With tears drawn from her eyes by your foul wrongs. / Myself, a prince by fortune of my birth, / Near to the King in blood, and near in love / Till you did make him misinterpret me, / Have stoop'd my neck under your injuries, / And sigh'd my English breath in foreign clouds, / Eating the bitter bread of banishment; / Whilst you have fed upon my signories, / Dispark'd my parks and felled my forest woods, / From my own windows torn my household coat, / Raz'd out my impress, leaving me no sign / Save men's opinions and my living blood / To show the world I am a gentleman. / This and much more, much more than twice all this, / Condemns you to the death. See them deliver'd over / To execution and the hand of death.

Bring these men out. Bushy and Green, I won't torment your souls, since they must leave your bodies very soon, by dwelling too much on your wicked lives; that would be unkind. But to wash your blood off my hands, I will set out here, in front of everyone, some of the reasons for your deaths. You have misled a prince, a royal king, a fortunate gentleman in birth and looks, whom you made unfortunate and completely spoiled. With your sinful pastimes you have more or less divorced him from his queen, broken up a royal marriage bed and stained the beauty of a fair queen's cheeks with tears your foul wrongs drew from her eyes. I myself, a prince by birth, close to the King in blood and close in love until you made him misjudge me, have bent my neck under the wrongs you did me and sighed my English breath into foreign clouds, eating the bitter bread of exile. Meanwhile you have fed on my estates, opened up my private parks and cut down my forests, torn my coat of arms out of my own windows and scratched out my emblem, leaving me no sign except people's opinion and my living blood to show the world I am a gentleman. This, and much more, much more than twice all this, condemns you to death. See that they are handed over for execution and the hand of death.
More welcome is the stroke of death to me / Than Bolingbroke to England. Lords, farewell.
The stroke of death is more welcome to me than Bolingbroke is to England. Lords, goodbye.
My comfort is that heaven will take our souls, / And plague injustice with the pains of hell.
My comfort is that heaven will take our souls and punish injustice with the pains of hell.
My Lord Northumberland, see them dispatch'd.
My Lord Northumberland, see that they are executed.
Uncle, you say the Queen is at your house; / For God's sake, fairly let her be entreated: / Tell her I send to her my kind commends; / Take special care my greetings be deliver'd.
Uncle, you say the Queen is at your house. For God's sake, see that she is treated well. Tell her I send her my kind regards. Take special care that my greetings are delivered.
A gentleman of mine I have dispatch'd / With letters of your love to her at large.
I have sent one of my gentlemen with a letter setting out your kind feelings towards her in full.
Thanks, gentle uncle. Come, lords, away, / To fight with Glendower and his complices. / Awhile to work, and after holiday.
Thank you, kind uncle. Come, lords, let's go to fight Glendower and his allies. A little work now, and a holiday afterwards.
Barkloughly Castle call they this at hand?
Is this the castle nearby they call Barkloughly?
Yea, my lord. How brooks your Grace the air / After your late tossing on the breaking seas?
Yes, my lord. How does your Grace like the air after being tossed about on the rough seas?

Needs must I like it well: I weep for joy / To stand upon my kingdom once again. / Dear earth, I do salute thee with my hand, / Though rebels wound thee with their horses' hoofs: / As a long-parted mother with her child / Plays fondly with her tears and smiles in meeting, / So weeping-smiling greet I thee, my earth, / And do thee favours with my royal hands. / Feed not thy sovereign's foe, my gentle earth, / Nor with thy sweets comfort his ravenous sense; / But let thy spiders, that suck up thy venom, / And heavy-gaited toads lie in their way, / Doing annoyance to the treacherous feet / Which with usurping steps do trample thee. / Yield stinging nettles to mine enemies; / And when they from thy bosom pluck a flower, / Guard it, I pray thee, with a lurking adder / Whose double tongue may with a mortal touch / Throw death upon thy sovereign's enemies. / Mock not my senseless conjuration, lords. / This earth shall have a feeling, and these stones / Prove armed soldiers, ere her native king / Shall falter under foul rebellion's arms.

I must like it very much. I weep for joy to stand on my kingdom once again. Dear earth, I greet you with my hand, though rebels wound you with their horses' hooves. Like a mother long separated from her child, who weeps and smiles tenderly when they meet, I greet you, my earth, weeping and smiling, and touch you lovingly with my royal hands. Don't feed your king's enemy, my gentle earth, and don't comfort his greedy appetite with your sweet things. Let your spiders, that suck up your poison, and slow, heavy toads lie in their path to trouble the treacherous feet that trample you with usurping steps. Grow stinging nettles for my enemies; and when they pick a flower from your breast, guard it, I beg you, with a hidden adder, whose forked tongue can throw death on your king's enemies with a deadly touch. Don't laugh at my appeal to things that can't feel, lords. This earth will come to have feelings, and these stones will turn into armed soldiers, before her rightful king is brought down by the weapons of foul rebellion.

Fear not, my lord; that Power that made you king / Hath power to keep you king in spite of all. / The means that heaven yields must be embrac'd / And not neglected; else, if heaven would, / And we will not, heaven's offer we refuse, / The proffer'd means of succour and redress.

Don't be afraid, my lord. The Power that made you king has the power to keep you king in spite of everything. But we must take hold of the means heaven gives us and not neglect them. Otherwise, if heaven is willing and we are not, we refuse what heaven offers, the means of help and rescue it holds out to us.
He means, my lord, that we are too remiss; / Whilst Bolingbroke, through our security, / Grows strong and great in substance and in friends.
He means, my lord, that we are too slack, while Bolingbroke grows strong and great in resources and friends because we feel too safe.

Discomfortable cousin! know'st thou not / That when the searching eye of heaven is hid, / Behind the globe, that lights the lower world, / Then thieves and robbers range abroad unseen / In murders and in outrage boldly here; / But when from under this terrestrial ball / He fires the proud tops of the eastern pines / And darts his light through every guilty hole, / Then murders, treasons, and detested sins, / The cloak of night being pluck'd from off their backs, / Stand bare and naked, trembling at themselves? / So when this thief, this traitor, Bolingbroke, / Who all this while hath revell'd in the night, / Whilst we were wandering with the Antipodes, / Shall see us rising in our throne, the east, / His treasons will sit blushing in his face, / Not able to endure the sight of day, / But self-affrighted tremble at his sin. / Not all the water in the rough rude sea / Can wash the balm off from an anointed king; / The breath of worldly men cannot depose / The deputy elected by the Lord. / For every man that Bolingbroke hath press'd / To lift shrewd steel against our golden crown, / God for his Richard hath in heavenly pay / A glorious angel: then, if angels fight, / Weak men must fall, for heaven still guards the right.

Gloomy cousin! Don't you know that when the searching eye of heaven, the sun, is hidden behind the earth and lights the world below, thieves and robbers wander about unseen, boldly committing murder and outrage here? But when he rises from under the earth, sets fire to the proud tops of the eastern pine trees and shoots his light into every guilty hole, then murders, treasons and hateful sins stand bare and naked, with the cloak of night pulled off their backs, trembling at themselves. So when this thief, this traitor Bolingbroke, who has been partying in the night all this time while we were wandering on the other side of the world, sees us rising on our throne in the east, his treasons will blush in his face. He will not be able to bear the sight of day, but will tremble, terrified, at his own sin. Not all the water in the rough, wild sea can wash the holy oil off an anointed king. The breath of mere earthly men cannot depose the deputy chosen by the Lord. For every man Bolingbroke has forced to raise his sharp steel against our golden crown, God has a glorious angel in heaven's pay for his Richard. Then if angels fight, weak men must fall, because heaven always guards the right.
Welcome, my lord. How far off lies your power?
Welcome, my lord. How far away is your army?

Nor near nor farther off, my gracious lord, / Than this weak arm: discomfort guides my tongue / And bids me speak of nothing but despair. / One day too late, I fear me, noble lord, / Hath clouded all thy happy days on earth. / O! call back yesterday, bid time return, / And thou shalt have twelve thousand fighting men! / To-day, to-day, unhappy day, too late, / O'erthrows thy joys, friends, fortune, and thy state; / For all the Welshmen, hearing thou wert dead, / Are gone to Bolingbroke, dispers'd, and fled.

No nearer and no further, my gracious lord, than this weak arm. Despair guides my tongue and tells me to speak of nothing but hopelessness. I fear, noble lord, that one day's delay has clouded all your happy days on earth. Oh, call back yesterday, tell time to turn back, and you will have twelve thousand fighting men! Today, today, this unlucky day, too late, overthrows your joys, friends, fortune and power; because all the Welshmen, hearing you were dead, have gone over to Bolingbroke, or scattered and run away.
Comfort, my liege! why looks your Grace so pale?
Courage, my lord! Why does your Grace look so pale?

But now, the blood of twenty thousand men / Did triumph in my face, and they are fled; / And till so much blood thither come again / Have I not reason to look pale and dead? / All souls that will be safe, fly from my side; / For time hath set a blot upon my pride.

Just now the blood of twenty thousand men glowed triumphantly in my face, and now they have run away. Until that much blood comes back there, don't I have good reason to look pale and dead? Let everyone who wants to be safe run from my side, because time has stained my pride.
Comfort, my liege! remember who you are.
Courage, my lord! Remember who you are.

I had forgot myself. Am I not king? / Awake, thou coward majesty! thou sleepest. / Is not the king's name twenty thousand names? / Arm, arm, my name! a puny subject strikes / At thy great glory. Look not to the ground, / Ye favourites of a king; are we not high? / High be our thoughts. I know my uncle York / Hath power enough to serve our turn. But who comes here?

I had forgotten myself. Am I not king? Wake up, you cowardly majesty! You are asleep. Isn't the king's name worth twenty thousand names? Arm yourself, arm yourself, my name! A puny subject is striking at your great glory. Don't look at the ground, you favourites of a king. Aren't we high? Let our thoughts be high. I know my uncle York has enough troops to do what we need. But who comes here?
More health and happiness betide my liege / Than can my care-tun'd tongue deliver him!
May more health and happiness come to my lord than my tongue, tuned to sad news, can bring him!

Mine ear is open and my heart prepar'd: / The worst is worldly loss thou canst unfold. / Say, is my kingdom lost? Why, 'twas my care, / And what loss is it to be rid of care? / Strives Bolingbroke to be as great as we? / Greater he shall not be: if he serve God / We'll serve him too, and be his fellow so: / Revolt our subjects? That we cannot mend; / They break their faith to God as well as us: / Cry woe, destruction, ruin, loss, decay; / The worst is death, and death will have his day.

My ear is open and my heart is ready. The worst you can tell me is a worldly loss. Tell me, is my kingdom lost? Well, it was my burden of care, and what loss is it to be rid of care? Is Bolingbroke trying to be as great as I am? He shall not be greater. If he serves God, I will serve God too, and so be his equal. Are my subjects rebelling? I can't put that right; they break their promises to God as well as to me. Cry woe, destruction, ruin, loss, decay. The worst is death, and death will have his day.

Glad am I that your highness is so arm'd / To bear the tidings of calamity. / Like an unseasonable stormy day / Which makes the silver rivers drown their shores, / As if the world were all dissolv'd to tears, / So high above his limits swells the rage / Of Bolingbroke, covering your fearful land / With hard bright steel and hearts harder than steel. / White-beards have arm'd their thin and hairless scalps / Against thy majesty; and boys, with women's voices, / Strive to speak big, and clap their female joints / In stiff unwieldy arms against thy crown; / Thy very beadsmen learn to bend their bows / Of double-fatal yew against thy state; / Yea, distaff-women manage rusty bills / Against thy seat: both young and old rebel, / And all goes worse than I have power to tell.

I am glad your highness is so well prepared to hear news of disaster. Like a stormy day out of season, that makes the silver rivers flood their banks as if the world had melted into tears, Bolingbroke's rage swells high above its limits, covering your frightened land with hard, bright steel and hearts harder than steel. White-bearded old men have put helmets on their thin, bald heads to fight your majesty. Boys with high voices try to speak like men and squeeze their soft limbs into stiff, heavy armour against your crown. Even the old men paid to pray for you learn to bend their bows of deadly yew against your rule. Even women who spin wool take up rusty spears against your throne. Young and old rebel, and everything is going worse than I can tell.

Too well, too well thou tell'st a tale so ill. / Where is the Earl of Wiltshire? Where is Bagot? / What is become of Bushy? Where is Green? / That they have let the dangerous enemy / Measure our confines with such peaceful steps? / If we prevail, their heads shall pay for it. / I warrant they have made peace with Bolingbroke.

You tell such a bad story far too well. Where is the Earl of Wiltshire? Where is Bagot? What has happened to Bushy? Where is Green? How have they let the dangerous enemy pace out our country so peacefully? If we win, their heads will pay for it. I bet they have made peace with Bolingbroke.
Peace have they made with him indeed, my lord.
They have made peace with him indeed, my lord.

O villains, vipers, damn'd without redemption! / Dogs, easily won to fawn on any man! / Snakes, in my heart-blood warm'd, that sting my heart! / Three Judases, each one thrice worse than Judas! / Would they make peace? Terrible hell make war / Upon their spotted souls for this offence!

Oh, villains, snakes, damned beyond saving! Dogs, easily won over to fawn on anyone! Snakes, warmed in my own heart's blood, who sting my heart! Three Judases, each one three times worse than Judas! Would they make peace? May terrible hell make war on their stained souls for this crime!

Sweet love, I see, changing his property, / Turns to the sourest and most deadly hate. / Again uncurse their souls; their peace is made / With heads, and not with hands: those whom you curse / Have felt the worst of death's destroying wound / And lie full low, grav'd in the hollow ground.

I see sweet love, when it changes its nature, turns into the sourest and deadliest hate. Take back your curses on their souls. They made their peace with their heads, not their hands. The men you curse have felt the worst of death's destroying wound and lie low, buried in the hollow ground.
Is Bushy, Green, and the Earl of Wiltshire dead?
Are Bushy, Green and the Earl of Wiltshire dead?
Ay, all of them at Bristol lost their heads.
Yes, they all lost their heads at Bristol.
Where is the Duke my father with his power?
Where is the Duke my father with his army?

No matter where. Of comfort no man speak: / Let's talk of graves, of worms, and epitaphs; / Make dust our paper, and with rainy eyes / Write sorrow on the bosom of the earth. / Let's choose executors and talk of wills; / And yet not so—for what can we bequeath / Save our deposed bodies to the ground? / Our lands, our lives, and all are Bolingbroke's. / And nothing can we call our own but death, / And that small model of the barren earth / Which serves as paste and cover to our bones. / For God's sake let us sit upon the ground / And tell sad stories of the death of kings: / How some have been deposed, some slain in war, / Some haunted by the ghosts they have depos'd, / Some poison'd by their wives, some sleeping kill'd; / All murder'd: for within the hollow crown / That rounds the mortal temples of a king / Keeps Death his court; and there the antick sits, / Scoffing his state and grinning at his pomp; / Allowing him a breath, a little scene, / To monarchize, be fear'd, and kill with looks, / Infusing him with self and vain conceit / As if this flesh which walls about our life / Were brass impregnable; and, humour'd thus, / Comes at the last, and with a little pin / Bores through his castle wall, and farewell, king! / Cover your heads, and mock not flesh and blood / With solemn reverence: throw away respect, / Tradition, form, and ceremonious duty; / For you have but mistook me all this while: / I live with bread like you, feel want, / Taste grief, need friends: subjected thus, / How can you say to me I am a king?

It doesn't matter where. Let nobody speak of comfort. Let's talk about graves, worms and epitaphs. Let's make the dust our paper and write sorrow on the breast of the earth with our rainy eyes. Let's choose executors and talk about wills. And yet, no: what can we leave except our deposed bodies to the ground? Our lands, our lives and everything belong to Bolingbroke, and we can call nothing our own except death and that small patch of barren earth that covers our bones like pastry over a pie. For God's sake, let's sit on the ground and tell sad stories about the deaths of kings: how some have been deposed, some killed in war, some haunted by the ghosts of those they deposed, some poisoned by their wives, some killed in their sleep. All murdered. Because inside the hollow crown that circles a king's mortal head, Death holds his court. There the clown sits, mocking the king's greatness and grinning at his ceremony, allowing him a breath, a short scene, to play the monarch, be feared and kill with a look, filling him with selfish, empty ideas, as if the flesh that walls in our life were unbreakable brass. And when he has amused himself like this, Death comes at last, and with a little pin he bores through the castle wall, and goodbye, king! Put your hats back on, and don't mock flesh and blood with solemn respect. Throw away respect, tradition, ceremony and formal duty, because you have misunderstood me all this time. I live on bread like you, feel need, taste grief, need friends. Since I am a subject to all these, how can you tell me I am a king?

My lord, wise men ne'er sit and wail their woes, / But presently prevent the ways to wail. / To fear the foe, since fear oppresseth strength, / Gives, in your weakness, strength unto your foe, / And so your follies fight against yourself. / Fear and be slain; no worse can come to fight; / And fight and die is death destroying death; / Where fearing dying pays death servile breath.

My lord, wise men never sit and moan about their troubles, but act at once to stop the causes of moaning. Fearing the enemy, since fear weakens strength, gives your enemy strength from your weakness, and so your foolishness fights against you. Be afraid, and you will be killed; nothing worse can come from fighting. To fight and die is to destroy death by death, while to die fearing death is to pay death the breath of a slave.
My father hath a power; inquire of him, / And learn to make a body of a limb.
My father has an army. Ask about him, and learn to make a whole body out of one limb.

Thou chid'st me well. Proud Bolingbroke, I come / To change blows with thee for our day of doom. / This ague fit of fear is over-blown; / An easy task it is to win our own.— / Say, Scroop, where lies our uncle with his power? / Speak sweetly, man, although thy looks be sour.

You scold me rightly. Proud Bolingbroke, I am coming to exchange blows with you and settle our fate. This shivering fit of fear has passed. It is an easy task to win back what is ours. Tell me, Scroop, where is our uncle with his army? Speak sweetly, man, even though you look sour.

Men judge by the complexion of the sky / The state in inclination of the day; / So may you by my dull and heavy eye, / My tongue hath but a heavier tale to say. / I play the torturer, by small and small / To lengthen out the worst that must be spoken: / Your uncle York is join'd with Bolingbroke; / And all your northern castles yielded up, / And all your southern gentlemen in arms / Upon his party.

Men judge what kind of day it will be by the colour of the sky. So you can judge by my dull, heavy eyes that my tongue only has a heavier story to tell. I am playing the torturer, dragging out bit by bit the worst news, which must be told. Your uncle York has joined Bolingbroke, all your northern castles have surrendered and all your southern gentlemen have taken up arms on his side.

Thou hast said enough. / [To AUMERLE] Beshrew thee, cousin, which didst lead me forth / Of that sweet way I was in to despair! / What say you now? What comfort have we now? / By heaven, I'll hate him everlastingly / That bids me be of comfort any more. / Go to Flint Castle; there I'll pine away; / A king, woe's slave, shall kingly woe obey. / That power I have, discharge; and let them go / To ear the land that hath some hope to grow, / For I have none. Let no man speak again / To alter this, for counsel is but vain.

You have said enough. Curse you, cousin, for leading me away from the sweet road to despair I was on! What do you say now? What comfort do we have now? By heaven, I will hate for ever anyone who tells me to take comfort again. Go to Flint Castle; I'll waste away there. A king who is sorrow's slave will obey royal sorrow. Dismiss the army I have, and let them go and plough land that has some hope of growing something, because I have none. Let no one speak again to change this, because advice is useless.
He does me double wrong / That wounds me with the flatteries of his tongue. / Discharge my followers; let them hence away, / From Richard's night to Bolingbroke's fair day.
Anyone who wounds me with the flattery of his tongue does me a double wrong. Dismiss my followers. Let them go away from Richard's night to Bolingbroke's bright day.
So that by this intelligence we learn / The Welshmen are dispers'd; and Salisbury / Is gone to meet the king, who lately landed / With some few private friends upon this coast.
So from this report we learn that the Welshmen have scattered, and Salisbury has gone to meet the king, who landed recently on this coast with a few close friends.
The news is very fair and good, my lord. / Richard not far from hence hath hid his head.
The news is very good, my lord. Richard has hidden his head not far from here.
It would beseem the Lord Northumberland / To say 'King Richard': alack the heavy day / When such a sacred king should hide his head!
It would be more fitting for Lord Northumberland to say 'King Richard'. Alas, what a sad day, when such a sacred king has to hide his head!
Your Grace mistakes; only to be brief, / Left I his title out.
Your Grace misunderstands. I left out his title only to be brief.
The time hath been, / Would you have been so brief with him, he would / Have been so brief with you to shorten you, / For taking so the head, your whole head's length.
There was a time when, if you had been so brief with him, he would have been brief with you and shortened you by a whole head's length for taking such liberties.
Mistake not, uncle, further than you should.
Don't take this the wrong way, uncle, any more than you should.
Take not, good cousin, further than you should, / Lest you mistake. The heavens are o'er our heads.
And don't you take more than you should, good nephew, or you may take the wrong way. The heavens are above our heads.
I know it, uncle; and oppose not myself / Against their will. But who comes here?
I know it, uncle, and I don't set myself against their will. But who is this?
Welcome, Harry: what, will not this castle yield?
Welcome, Harry. What, won't this castle surrender?
The castle royally is mann'd, my lord, / Against thy entrance.
The castle is royally defended against you, my lord.
Royally! / Why, it contains no king?
Royally! Why, there's no king in it, is there?

Yes, my good lord, / It doth contain a king; King Richard lies / Within the limits of yon lime and stone; / And with him are the Lord Aumerle, Lord Salisbury, / Sir Stephen Scroop, besides a clergyman / Of holy reverence; who, I cannot learn.

Yes, my good lord, there is a king inside. King Richard is within those walls of lime and stone over there, and with him are Lord Aumerle, Lord Salisbury, Sir Stephen Scroop and a holy clergyman; I can't find out who.
O! belike it is the Bishop of Carlisle.
Oh, it's probably the Bishop of Carlisle.

[To NORTHUMBERLAND] Noble lord, / Go to the rude ribs of that ancient castle; / Through brazen trumpet send the breath of parley / Into his ruin'd ears, and thus deliver: / Henry Bolingbroke / On both his knees doth kiss King Richard's hand, / And sends allegiance and true faith of heart / To his most royal person; hither come / Even at his feet to lay my arms and power, / Provided that my banishment repeal'd / And lands restor'd again be freely granted; / If not, I'll use the advantage of my power / And lay the summer's dust with showers of blood / Rain'd from the wounds of slaughtered Englishmen; / The which, how far off from the mind of Bolingbroke / It is, such crimson tempest should bedrench / The fresh green lap of fair King Richard's land, / My stooping duty tenderly shall show. / Go, signify as much, while here we march / Upon the grassy carpet of this plain. / Let's march without the noise of threat'ning drum, / That from this castle's totter'd battlements / Our fair appointments may be well perus'd. / Methinks King Richard and myself should meet / With no less terror than the elements / Of fire and water, when their thund'ring shock / At meeting tears the cloudy cheeks of heaven. / Be he the fire, I'll be the yielding water; / The rage be his, whilst on the earth I rain / My waters; on the earth, and not on him. / March on, and mark King Richard how he looks.

Noble lord, go to the rough walls of that ancient castle. Send the breath of a request to talk through a brass trumpet into its broken ears, and deliver this message: Henry Bolingbroke kisses King Richard's hand on both knees and sends loyalty and true faith of heart to his most royal person. I have come here to lay my weapons and my army at his feet, on condition that my banishment is cancelled and my lands are given back freely. If not, I will use the advantage of my strength and settle the summer's dust with showers of blood rained from the wounds of slaughtered Englishmen. My humble kneeling will gently show how far it is from Bolingbroke's mind that such a crimson storm should soak the fresh green lap of fair King Richard's land. Go and tell him this, while we march here on the grassy carpet of this plain. Let's march without the threatening noise of drums, so that our fine equipment can be clearly seen from the castle's crumbling walls. I think King Richard and I should meet with no less terror than the elements of fire and water, when their thundering clash tears the cloudy cheeks of the sky. Let him be the fire, and I'll be the water that gives way. Let the rage be his, while I rain my waters on the earth; on the earth, not on him. March on, and watch how King Richard looks.

See, see, King Richard doth himself appear, / As doth the blushing discontented sun / From out the fiery portal of the east, / When he perceives the envious clouds are bent / To dim his glory and to stain the track / Of his bright passage to the occident.

Look, look, King Richard appears himself, like the blushing, unhappy sun coming out of the fiery gateway of the east, when he sees that jealous clouds are set on dimming his glory and staining the path of his bright journey to the west.
Yet he looks like a king: behold, his eye, / As bright as is the eagle's, lightens forth / Controlling majesty: alack, alack, for woe, / That any harm should stain so fair a show!
And yet he looks like a king. Look, his eye, as bright as an eagle's, flashes out commanding majesty. Alas, alas, how sad that any harm should stain such a fine sight!

[To NORTHUMBERLAND] We are amaz'd; and thus long have we stood / To watch the fearful bending of thy knee, / Because we thought ourself thy lawful king; / And if we be, how dare thy joints forget / To pay their awful duty to our presence? / If we be not, show us the hand of God / That hath dismiss'd us from our stewardship; / For well we know no hand of blood and bone / Can gripe the sacred handle of our sceptre, / Unless he do profane, steal, or usurp. / And though you think that all, as you have done, / Have torn their souls by turning them from us, / And we are barren and bereft of friends, / Yet know, my master, God omnipotent, / Is mustering in his clouds on our behalf / Armies of pestilence; and they shall strike / Your children yet unborn and unbegot, / That lift your vassal hands against my head / And threat the glory of my precious crown. / Tell Bolingbroke,—for yond methinks he stands,— / That every stride he makes upon my land / Is dangerous treason; he is come to open / The purple testament of bleeding war; / But ere the crown he looks for live in peace, / Ten thousand bloody crowns of mothers' sons / Shall ill become the flower of England's face, / Change the complexion of her maid-pale peace / To scarlet indignation, and bedew / Her pastures' grass with faithful English blood.

I am astonished. I have stood here this long waiting to see you bend your knee in fear, because I thought I was your lawful king. And if I am, how dare your joints forget to pay their respectful duty to my presence? If I am not, show me the hand of God that has dismissed me from my office, because I know well that no hand of flesh and blood can grip the sacred handle of my sceptre without committing sacrilege, theft or usurpation. And though you think that everyone has torn their souls, as you have, by turning them away from me, and that I am left bare and without friends, know this: my master, almighty God, is gathering armies of plague in his clouds on my behalf. They will strike your children, not yet born or even conceived, because you lift your servants' hands against my head and threaten the glory of my precious crown. Tell Bolingbroke, for I think that's him standing there, that every step he takes on my land is dangerous treason. He has come to open the blood-red will of bleeding war. But before the crown he is after can live in peace, ten thousand bloody heads of mothers' sons will spoil the flower of England's face, change the pale, maiden colour of her peace to scarlet anger, and wet the grass of her fields with loyal English blood.

The King of Heaven forbid our lord the King / Should so with civil and uncivil arms / Be rush'd upon! Thy thrice noble cousin, / Harry Bolingbroke, doth humbly kiss thy hand; / And by the honourable tomb he swears / That stands upon your royal grandsire's bones, / And by the royalties of both your bloods, / Currents that spring from one most gracious head, / And by the buried hand of warlike Gaunt, / And by the worth and honour of himself, / Comprising all that may be sworn or said, / His coming hither hath no further scope / Than for his lineal royalties, and to beg / Enfranchisement immediate on his knees; / Which on thy royal party granted once, / His glittering arms he will commend to rust, / His barbed steeds to stables, and his heart / To faithful service of your Majesty. / This swears he, as he is a prince, is just; / And as I am a gentleman I credit him.

The King of Heaven forbid that our lord the King should be attacked like this with weapons of civil war! Your thrice-noble cousin, Harry Bolingbroke, humbly kisses your hand. He swears by the honourable tomb that stands over your royal grandfather's bones, by the royal blood of you both, two streams springing from one most gracious source, by the buried hand of warlike Gaunt, and by his own worth and honour, which covers everything that can be sworn or said, that his only purpose in coming here is to claim his inherited titles and to beg on his knees to have his rights restored at once. Once your Majesty grants that, he will leave his glittering weapons to rust, his armoured horses to their stables and his heart to faithful service of your Majesty. He swears this is fair, on his word as a prince; and on my word as a gentleman, I believe him.

Northumberland, say, thus the king returns: / His noble cousin is right welcome hither; / And all the number of his fair demands / Shall be accomplish'd without contradiction. / With all the gracious utterance thou hast / Speak to his gentle hearing kind commends.

Northumberland, tell him that this is the king's reply: his noble cousin is very welcome here, and all his reasonable demands will be met without argument. With all the courteous words you have, give him my kind regards.
[To AUMERLE] We do debase ourselves, cousin, do we not, / To look so poorly and to speak so fair? / Shall we call back Northumberland, and send / Defiance to the traitor, and so die?
Cousin, aren't we lowering ourselves by looking so poor and speaking so politely? Shall we call Northumberland back, send defiance to the traitor and so die?
No, good my lord; let's fight with gentle words / Till time lend friends, and friends their helpful swords.
No, my good lord. Let's fight with gentle words until time gives us friends, and friends give us their helpful swords.

O God, O God! that e'er this tongue of mine / That laid the sentence of dread banishment / On yond proud man should take it off again / With words of sooth! O! that I were as great / As is my grief, or lesser than my name, / Or that I could forget what I have been, / Or not remember what I must be now. / Swell'st thou, proud heart? I'll give thee scope to beat, / Since foes have scope to beat both thee and me.

O God, O God, that this tongue of mine, which passed the terrible sentence of exile on that proud man over there, should ever take it off again with flattering words! Oh, I wish I were as great as my grief, or less than my title, or that I could forget what I have been, or not remember what I must be now! Are you swelling, proud heart? I'll give you room to beat, since my enemies have room to beat both you and me.
Northumberland is coming back from Bolingbroke.

What must the King do now? Must he submit? / The king shall do it: must he be depos'd? / The king shall be contented: must he lose / The name of king? A God's name, let it go: / I'll give my jewels for a set of beads, / My gorgeous palace for a hermitage, / My gay apparel for an almsman's gown, / My figur'd goblets for a dish of wood, / My sceptre for a palmer's walking-staff, / My subjects for a pair of carved saints, / And my large kingdom for a little grave, / A little little grave, an obscure grave; / Or I'll be buried in the king's highway, / Some way of common trade, where subjects' feet / May hourly trample on their sovereign's head; / For on my heart they tread now whilst I live; / And buried once, why not upon my head? / Aumerle, thou weep'st, my tender-hearted cousin! / We'll make foul weather with despised tears; / Our sighs and they shall lodge the summer corn / And make a dearth in this revolting land. / Or shall we play the wantons with our woes / And make some pretty match with shedding tears? / As thus: to drop them still upon one place / Till they have fretted us a pair of graves / Within the earth; and, there inlaid: 'There lies / Two kinsmen digg'd their graves with weeping eyes.' / Would not this ill do well? Well, well, I see / I talk but idly, and you laugh at me. / Most mighty prince, my Lord Northumberland, / What says King Bolingbroke? will his Majesty / Give Richard leave to live till Richard die? / You make a leg, and Bolingbroke says ay.

What must the King do now? Must he give in? The king will do it. Must he be deposed? The king will be content. Must he lose the name of king? In God's name, let it go. I'll give my jewels for a string of prayer beads, my splendid palace for a hermit's cell, my fine clothes for a beggar's gown, my engraved goblets for a wooden bowl, my sceptre for a pilgrim's walking stick, my subjects for a pair of carved saints, and my large kingdom for a little grave, a little, little grave, an unknown grave. Or I'll be buried in the king's highway, some busy road, where subjects' feet can trample on their king's head every hour; because they tread on my heart now while I'm alive, so once I'm buried, why not on my head? Aumerle, you're crying, my tender-hearted cousin! We'll make bad weather with our despised tears. Our sighs and tears together will flatten the summer corn and cause a famine in this rebellious country. Or shall we play games with our sorrows and have a pretty contest in shedding tears? Like this: we drop them on the same spot until they have worn a pair of graves for us in the earth, with this carved there: 'Here lie two relatives who dug their graves with weeping eyes.' Wouldn't this misery work well? Well, well, I see I'm just talking nonsense, and you are laughing at me. Most mighty prince, my Lord Northumberland, what does King Bolingbroke say? Will his Majesty give Richard permission to live until Richard dies? You bow, and that means Bolingbroke says yes.
My lord, in the base court he doth attend / To speak with you; may it please you to come down?
My lord, he is waiting in the lower courtyard to speak with you. Would you be pleased to come down?

Down, down I come; like glist'ring Phaethon, / Wanting the manage of unruly jades. / In the base court? Base court, where kings grow base, / To come at traitors' calls, and do them grace. / In the base court? Come down? Down, court! down, king! / For night-owls shriek where mounting larks should sing.

Down, down I come, like glittering Phaethon, unable to control his wild horses. In the lower courtyard? The low court, where kings become low, coming when traitors call and doing them honour. In the lower courtyard? Come down? Down, court! Down, king! For night owls shriek where rising larks should sing.
Sorrow and grief of heart / Makes him speak fondly, like a frantic man; / Yet he is come.
Sorrow and grief of heart make him talk foolishly, like a madman. But he is coming.
Stand all apart, / And show fair duty to his Majesty. [Kneeling] / My gracious lord,—
Everyone stand back and show proper respect to his Majesty. My gracious lord...

Fair cousin, you debase your princely knee / To make the base earth proud with kissing it: / Me rather had my heart might feel your love / Than my unpleas'd eye see your courtesy. / Up, cousin, up; your heart is up, I know, / Thus high at least, although your knee be low.

Fair cousin, you lower your princely knee by making the low earth proud by kissing it. I would rather my heart could feel your love than my displeased eye see your politeness. Up, cousin, up. I know your heart is up, at least this high, though your knee is low.
My gracious lord, I come but for mine own.
My gracious lord, I have come only for what is mine.
Your own is yours, and I am yours, and all.
What is yours is yours, and I am yours, and everything is.
So far be mine, my most redoubted lord, / As my true service shall deserve your love.
Let me have only as much, my most feared lord, as my true service deserves from your love.

Well you deserve: they well deserve to have / That know the strong'st and surest way to get. / Uncle, give me your hand: nay, dry your eyes: / Tears show their love, but want their remedies. / Cousin, I am too young to be your father, / Though you are old enough to be my heir. / What you will have, I'll give, and willing too; / For do we must what force will have us do. / Set on towards London. Cousin, is it so?

You deserve it well. Those who know the strongest and surest way to get things deserve to have them. Uncle, give me your hand. No, dry your eyes. Tears show love, but they can't cure anything. Cousin, I am too young to be your father, though you are old enough to be my heir. What you want, I will give you, and willingly too, because we must do what force makes us do. Set off towards London. Cousin, is that right?
Then I must not say no.
Then I must not say no.
What sport shall we devise here in this garden / To drive away the heavy thought of care?
What game can we think up here in this garden to drive away heavy, worried thoughts?
'Twill make me think the world is full of rubs / And that my fortune runs against the bias.
It will make me think the world is full of obstacles, and my fortune runs off course.
My legs can keep no measure in delight, / When my poor heart no measure keeps in grief: / Therefore no dancing, girl; some other sport.
My legs can't keep time with delight when my poor heart keeps no limit in its grief. So no dancing, girl. Some other game.

Of neither, girl: / For if of joy, being altogether wanting, / It doth remember me the more of sorrow; / Or if of grief, being altogether had, / It adds more sorrow to my want of joy; / For what I have I need not to repeat, / And what I want it boots not to complain.

Neither, girl. If they are about joy, which I have none of, they will only remind me more of sorrow. If they are about grief, which I have plenty of, they will add more sorrow to my lack of joy. What I have, I don't need to repeat; and what I lack, it does no good to complain about.
'Tis well that thou hast cause; / But thou shouldst please me better wouldst thou weep.
It's good that you have reason to; but you would please me more if you would cry.
I could weep, madam, would it do you good.
I could cry, madam, if it would do you good.

And I could sing, would weeping do me good, / And never borrow any tear of thee. / But stay, here come the gardeners. / Let's step into the shadow of these trees. / My wretchedness unto a row of pins, / They will talk of state, for every one doth so / Against a change: woe is forerun with woe.

And I could sing, if crying would do me any good, and never need to borrow a tear from you. But wait, here come the gardeners. Let's step into the shade of these trees. I'll bet my misery against a row of pins that they'll talk about politics; everyone does when a change is coming. Sorrow is always announced by sorrow.

Go, bind thou up yon dangling apricocks, / Which, like unruly children, make their sire / Stoop with oppression of their prodigal weight: / Give some supportance to the bending twigs. / Go thou, and like an executioner / Cut off the heads of too fast growing sprays / That look too lofty in our commonwealth: / All must be even in our government. / You thus employ'd, I will go root away / The noisome weeds which without profit suck / The soil's fertility from wholesome flowers.

You, go and tie up those dangling apricots over there, which, like unruly children, make their father bend under their heavy, wasteful weight. Give some support to the bending branches. You go, and like an executioner cut off the heads of the shoots that grow too fast and look too high in our little state. Everything must be level in our government. While you do that, I will go and dig up the harmful weeds that uselessly suck the soil's goodness away from the healthy flowers.

Why should we in the compass of a pale / Keep law and form and due proportion, / Showing, as in a model, our firm estate, / When our sea-walled garden, the whole land, / Is full of weeds; her fairest flowers chok'd up, / Her fruit trees all unprun'd, her hedges ruin'd, / Her knots disordered, and her wholesome herbs / Swarming with caterpillars?

Why should we keep law, order and proper balance inside the fence of this garden, showing a model of a well-run state, when our sea-walled garden, the whole country, is full of weeds, her finest flowers choked, her fruit trees unpruned, her hedges ruined, her flower beds in a mess and her healthy herbs crawling with caterpillars?
