Hold thy peace. / He that hath suffer'd this disorder'd spring / Hath now himself met with the fall of leaf; / The weeds which his broad-spreading leaves did shelter, / That seem'd in eating him to hold him up, / Are pluck'd up root and all by Bolingbroke; / I mean the Earl of Wiltshire, Bushy, Green.

Be quiet. The man who allowed this disordered spring has now met his own autumn. The weeds that his wide leaves sheltered, which seemed to hold him up while they were eating him, have been pulled up, roots and all, by Bolingbroke. I mean the Earl of Wiltshire, Bushy and Green.

They are; and Bolingbroke / Hath seiz'd the wasteful King. O! what pity is it / That he had not so trimm'd and dress'd his land / As we this garden! We at time of year / Do wound the bark, the skin of our fruit trees, / Lest, being over-proud in sap and blood, / With too much riches it confound itself: / Had he done so to great and growing men, / They might have liv'd to bear, and he to taste / Their fruits of duty: superfluous branches / We lop away, that bearing boughs may live: / Had he done so, himself had borne the crown, / Which waste of idle hours hath quite thrown down.

They are, and Bolingbroke has captured the wasteful King. Oh, what a pity it is that he didn't trim and tend his land as we do this garden! At the right time of year we cut the bark, the skin of our fruit trees, in case they get too full of sap and blood and destroy themselves with too much richness. If he had done that to great men who were growing too powerful, they might have lived to bear fruit, and he to taste their fruits of loyalty. We cut off unnecessary branches so that fruit-bearing boughs can live. If he had done that, he would still be wearing the crown, which the waste of idle hours has completely thrown down.
What! think you the king shall be depos'd?
What! Do you think the king will be deposed?
Depress'd he is already, and depos'd / 'Tis doubt he will be: letters came last night / To a dear friend of the good Duke of York's / That tell black tidings.
He's brought low already, and it's likely he will be deposed. Letters came last night to a close friend of the good Duke of York with dark news.
O! I am press'd to death through want of speaking!
Oh, I am being crushed to death because I can't speak!

Thou, old Adam's likeness, set to dress this garden, / How dares thy harsh rude tongue sound this unpleasing news? / What Eve, what serpent, hath suggested thee / To make a second fall of cursed man? / Why dost thou say King Richard is depos'd? / Dar'st thou, thou little better thing than earth, / Divine his downfall? Say, where, when, and how, / Cam'st thou by this ill tidings? Speak, thou wretch.

You, made in the image of old Adam, put here to look after this garden, how dare your harsh, rough tongue tell this unpleasant news? What Eve, what serpent, has tempted you to make cursed mankind fall a second time? Why do you say King Richard is deposed? Do you dare, you thing little better than dirt, to foretell his downfall? Tell me, where, when and how did you hear this bad news? Speak, you wretch.

Pardon me, madam: little joy have I / To breathe this news; yet what I say is true. / King Richard, he is in the mighty hold / Of Bolingbroke: their fortunes both are weigh'd. / In your lord's scale is nothing but himself, / And some few vanities that make him light; / But in the balance of great Bolingbroke, / Besides himself, are all the English peers, / And with that odds he weighs King Richard down. / Post you to London, and you will find it so; / I speak no more than every one doth know.

Forgive me, madam. I take little pleasure in telling this news, but what I say is true. King Richard is in Bolingbroke's powerful grip. Their fortunes have been weighed. In your husband's scale there is nothing but himself and a few vanities that make him light. But in great Bolingbroke's scale, besides himself, there are all the English lords, and with that advantage he weighs King Richard down. Hurry to London and you will find it is true. I'm saying no more than everyone knows.

Nimble mischance, that art so light of foot, / Doth not thy embassage belong to me, / And am I last that knows it? O! thou thinkest / To serve me last, that I may longest keep / Thy sorrow in my breast. Come, ladies, go, / To meet at London London's king in woe. / What was I born to this, that my sad look / Should grace the triumph of great Bolingbroke? / Gardener, for telling me these news of woe, / Pray God the plants thou graft'st may never grow!

Quick misfortune, so light on your feet, isn't your message meant for me, and am I the last to know it? Oh, you think you'll serve me last so that I keep your sorrow in my heart the longest. Come, ladies, let's go and meet London's king, sorrowful in London. Was I born for this, so that my sad face should decorate great Bolingbroke's triumph? Gardener, for telling me this sad news, I pray God that the plants you graft may never grow!

Poor Queen, so that thy state might be no worse, / I would my skill were subject to thy curse. / Here did she fall a tear; here in this place / I'll set a bank of rue, sour herb of grace. / Rue, even for ruth, here shortly shall be seen, / In the remembrance of a weeping queen.

Poor Queen, if it would keep your situation from getting worse, I'd be happy for my skill to suffer your curse. Here she dropped a tear. Here in this place I'll plant a bed of rue, the bitter herb of grace. Rue, standing for pity, will soon be seen here in memory of a weeping queen.
Call forth Bagot. / Now, Bagot, freely speak thy mind; / What thou dost know of noble Gloucester's death; / Who wrought it with the King, and who perform'd / The bloody office of his timeless end.

Bring Bagot forward. Now, Bagot, speak freely. Tell us what you know about noble Gloucester's death: who worked with the King to bring it about, and who carried out the bloody job of killing him before his time.
Then set before my face the Lord Aumerle.
Then put the Lord Aumerle in front of me.
Cousin, stand forth, and look upon that man.
Cousin, step forward and look at that man.

My Lord Aumerle, I know your daring tongue / Scorns to unsay what once it hath deliver'd. / In that dead time when Gloucester's death was plotted / I heard you say 'Is not my arm of length, / That reacheth from the restful English Court / As far as Calais, to mine uncle's head?' / Amongst much other talk that very time / I heard you say that you had rather refuse / The offer of an hundred thousand crowns / Than Bolingbroke's return to England; / Adding withal, how blest this land would be / In this your cousin's death.

My Lord Aumerle, I know your bold tongue is too proud to take back what it has once said. At that dark time when Gloucester's death was being plotted, I heard you say, 'Isn't my arm long enough to reach from the peaceful English court as far as Calais, to my uncle's head?' In a lot of other talk at that very time, I heard you say you would rather turn down a hundred thousand crowns than see Bolingbroke come back to England, and you added how blessed this country would be if your cousin died.

Princes, and noble lords, / What answer shall I make to this base man? / Shall I so much dishonour my fair stars / On equal terms to give him chastisement? / Either I must, or have mine honour soil'd / With the attainder of his slanderous lips. / There is my gage, the manual seal of death / That marks thee out for hell: I say thou liest, / And will maintain what thou hast said is false / In thy heart-blood, through being all too base / To stain the temper of my knightly sword.

Princes and noble lords, what answer shall I give this lowborn man? Shall I so dishonour my noble birth as to fight him as an equal? Either I must, or let my honour be stained by the accusation of his slandering lips. There is my glove, the hand-sealed warrant of death that marks you out for hell. I say you lie, and I will prove that what you have said is false with your heart's blood, though it is much too lowly to stain my knightly sword.
Bagot, forbear; thou shalt not take it up.
Bagot, stop. You shall not pick it up.
Excepting one, I would he were the best / In all this presence that hath mov'd me so.
Except for one man, I wish the one who has provoked me like this were the noblest man here.

If that thy valour stand on sympathies, / There is my gage, Aumerle, in gage to thine: / By that fair sun which shows me where thou stand'st, / I heard thee say, and vauntingly thou spak'st it, / That thou wert cause of noble Gloucester's death. / If thou deny'st it twenty times, thou liest; / And I will turn thy falsehood to thy heart, / Where it was forged, with my rapier's point.

If your courage needs an equal in rank, there is my glove, Aumerle, as a challenge to yours. By that bright sun that shows me where you stand, I heard you say, and you said it boastfully, that you caused noble Gloucester's death. If you deny it twenty times, you lie; and I will drive your lie back into your heart, where it was made, with the point of my sword.
Thou darest not, coward, live to see that day.
You don't dare live to see that day, coward.
Now, by my soul, I would it were this hour.
Now, by my soul, I wish it were this very hour.
Fitzwater, thou art damn'd to hell for this.
Fitzwater, you are damned to hell for this.

Aumerle, thou liest; his honour is as true / In this appeal as thou art an unjust; / And that thou art so, there I throw my gage, / To prove it on thee to the extremest point / Of mortal breathing: seize it if thou dar'st.
Aumerle, you lie. His honour is as true in this accusation as you are false; and to prove you are, there I throw my glove, to prove it on you to the last breath of life. Pick it up if you dare.
And if I do not, may my hands rot off / And never brandish more revengeful steel / Over the glittering helmet of my foe!
And if I don't, may my hands rot off and never again swing a revengeful sword over the glittering helmet of my enemy!

I task the earth to the like, forsworn Aumerle; / And spur thee on with full as many lies / As may be halloa'd in thy treacherous ear / From sun to sun: there is my honour's pawn; / Engage it to the trial if thou dar'st.

I load the earth with the same challenge, perjured Aumerle, and spur you on with as many accusations of lying as can be shouted into your treacherous ear from sunrise to sunset. There is the pledge of my honour. Take it up for the trial if you dare.
Who sets me else? By heaven, I'll throw at all: / I have a thousand spirits in one breast / To answer twenty thousand such as you.
Who else challenges me? By heaven, I'll take on everyone. I have a thousand spirits in one heart to answer twenty thousand men like you.
My Lord Fitzwater, I do remember well / The very time Aumerle and you did talk.
My Lord Fitzwater, I remember very well the exact time Aumerle and you talked.
'Tis very true: you were in presence then, / And you can witness with me this is true.
That's quite true. You were there then, and you can back me up that this is true.
As false, by heaven, as heaven itself is true.
It is as false, by heaven, as heaven itself is true.

Dishonourable boy! / That lie shall lie so heavy on my sword / That it shall render vengeance and revenge / Till thou the lie-giver and that lie do lie / In earth as quiet as thy father's skull. / In proof whereof, there is my honour's pawn; / Engage it to the trial if thou dar'st.

Dishonourable boy! That lie will lie so heavily on my sword that it will pay back vengeance and revenge until you, the giver of the lie, and your lie lie in the earth as quiet as your father's skull. To prove it, there is the pledge of my honour. Take it up for the trial if you dare.

How fondly dost thou spur a forward horse! / If I dare eat, or drink, or breathe, or live, / I dare meet Surrey in a wilderness, / And spit upon him, whilst I say he lies, / And lies, and lies: there is my bond of faith / To tie thee to my strong correction. / As I intend to thrive in this new world, / Aumerle is guilty of my true appeal: / Besides, I heard the banish'd Norfolk say / That thou, Aumerle, didst send two of thy men / To execute the noble duke at Calais.

How foolishly you spur on a horse that is already eager! If I dare to eat or drink or breathe or live, I dare to meet Surrey in a wilderness and spit on him while I say he lies, and lies, and lies. There is my pledge of honour to bind you to the harsh punishment I'll give you. As I hope to prosper in this new world, Aumerle is guilty of what I truly accuse him of. Besides, I heard the banished Norfolk say that you, Aumerle, sent two of your men to kill the noble duke at Calais.
Some honest Christian trust me with a gage. / That Norfolk lies, here do I throw down this, / If he may be repeal'd to try his honour.
Will some honest Christian lend me a glove? I throw this down to prove that Norfolk lies, if he can be called back to defend his honour.

These differences shall all rest under gage / Till Norfolk be repeal'd: repeal'd he shall be / And, though mine enemy, restor'd again / To all his lands and signories; when he is return'd, / Against Aumerle we will enforce his trial.

These quarrels will all remain under challenge until Norfolk is called back. He shall be called back and, though he is my enemy, given back all his lands and estates. When he has returned, we will make him face Aumerle in trial by combat.

That honourable day shall ne'er be seen. / Many a time hath banish'd Norfolk fought / For Jesu Christ in glorious Christian field, / Streaming the ensign of the Christian cross / Against black pagans, Turks, and Saracens; / And, toil'd with works of war, retir'd himself / To Italy; and there, at Venice, gave / His body to that pleasant country's earth, / And his pure soul unto his captain, Christ, / Under whose colours he had fought so long.

That honourable day will never be seen. Banished Norfolk fought many times for Jesus Christ on glorious Christian battlefields, flying the banner of the Christian cross against black pagans, Turks and Saracens. Then, worn out by the labours of war, he retired to Italy, and there, at Venice, he gave his body to that pleasant country's earth and his pure soul to his captain, Christ, under whose flag he had fought for so long.
As surely as I live, my lord.
As surely as I am alive, my lord.
Sweet peace conduct his sweet soul to the bosom / Of good old Abraham! Lords appellants, / Your differences shall all rest under gage / Till we assign you to your days of trial

May sweet peace lead his sweet soul to the arms of good old Abraham in heaven! Lords who have made these accusations, your quarrels will all remain under challenge until we give you days for your trials.

Great Duke of Lancaster, I come to thee / From plume-pluck'd Richard; who with willing soul / Adopts thee heir, and his high sceptre yields / To the possession of thy royal hand. / Ascend his throne, descending now from him; / And long live Henry, of that name the fourth!

Great Duke of Lancaster, I come to you from Richard, stripped of his feathers, who willingly adopts you as his heir and hands over his high sceptre to your royal hand. Climb up to his throne, which he is now climbing down from; and long live Henry, the fourth king of that name!
In God's name, I'll ascend the regal throne.
In God's name, I'll climb up to the royal throne.

Marry, God forbid! / Worst in this royal presence may I speak, / Yet best beseeming me to speak the truth. / Would God that any in this noble presence / Were enough noble to be upright judge / Of noble Richard! Then true noblesse would / Learn him forbearance from so foul a wrong. / What subject can give sentence on his king? / And who sits here that is not Richard's subject? / Thieves are not judg'd but they are by to hear, / Although apparent guilt be seen in them; / And shall the figure of God's majesty, / His captain, steward, deputy elect, / Anointed, crowned, planted many years, / Be judg'd by subject and inferior breath, / And he himself not present? O! forfend it, God, / That in a Christian climate souls refin'd / Should show so heinous, black, obscene a deed! / I speak to subjects, and a subject speaks, / Stirr'd up by God, thus boldly for his king. / My Lord of Hereford here, whom you call king, / Is a foul traitor to proud Hereford's king; / And if you crown him, let me prophesy, / The blood of English shall manure the ground / And future ages groan for this foul act; / Peace shall go sleep with Turks and infidels, / And in this seat of peace tumultuous wars / Shall kin with kin and kind with kind confound; / Disorder, horror, fear, and mutiny, / Shall here inhabit, and this land be call'd / The field of Golgotha and dead men's skulls. / O! if you raise this house against this house, / It will the woefullest division prove / That ever fell upon this cursed earth. / Prevent it, resist it, let it not be so, / Lest child, child's children, cry against you 'woe!'

God forbid! I may be the lowest in this royal company to speak, but I am the most fitting one to speak the truth. I wish to God anyone in this noble company were noble enough to be a fair judge of noble Richard! Then true nobility would teach him to hold back from such a foul wrong. What subject can pass sentence on his king? And who sits here who is not Richard's subject? Thieves are not judged unless they are there to hear it, even when their guilt is obvious. And shall the image of God's majesty, his captain, steward and chosen deputy, anointed, crowned and established for many years, be judged by the voices of his subjects and inferiors, without even being present himself? Oh, God forbid that in a Christian country refined souls should commit such a hateful, black, disgusting deed! I am speaking to subjects, and a subject is speaking, stirred up by God to speak out like this for his king. My Lord of Hereford here, whom you call king, is a foul traitor to proud Hereford's king. And if you crown him, let me prophesy: English blood will fertilise the ground, and future ages will groan because of this foul act. Peace will go to sleep among Turks and unbelievers, and in this home of peace, violent wars will set relatives against relatives and countrymen against countrymen. Disorder, horror, fear and rebellion will live here, and this country will be called Golgotha, the field of dead men's skulls. Oh, if you raise this royal house against this house, it will be the most terrible division that ever fell on this cursed earth. Prevent it, resist it, don't let it happen, or your children and your children's children will cry 'woe' against you!

Well have you argued, sir; and, for your pains, / Of capital treason we arrest you here. / My Lord of Westminster, be it your charge / To keep him safely till his day of trial. / May it please you, lords, to grant the commons' suit?

You have argued well, sir; and for your trouble, we arrest you here for high treason. My Lord of Westminster, I put you in charge of keeping him safe until his trial. Lords, will you grant the request of the Commons?
Fetch hither Richard, that in common view / He may surrender; so we shall proceed / Without suspicion.
Bring Richard here, so that he can surrender in front of everyone. That way we can go ahead without anyone suspecting us.
Lords, you that here are under our arrest, / Procure your sureties for your days of answer. / Little are we beholding to your love, / And little look'd for at your helping hands.
Lords, those of you who are under arrest here, find people to guarantee you will appear on your trial days. We owe little to your love, and we expected little help from your hands.

Alack! why am I sent for to a king / Before I have shook off the regal thoughts / Wherewith I reign'd? I hardly yet have learn'd / To insinuate, flatter, bow, and bend my knee. / Give sorrow leave awhile to tutor me / To this submission. Yet I well remember / The favours of these men: were they not mine? / Did they not sometime cry 'All hail!' to me? / So Judas did to Christ: but he, in twelve, / Found truth in all but one; I, in twelve thousand, none. / God save the King! Will no man say, amen? / Am I both priest and clerk? Well then, amen. / God save the King! although I be not he; / And yet, amen, if heaven do think him me. / To do what service am I sent for hither?

Alas, why am I sent for to come to a king before I have shaken off the royal thoughts I reigned with? I have hardly learned yet how to creep, flatter, bow and bend my knee. Give sorrow a little time to teach me this submission. And yet I remember these men's faces well. Weren't they mine? Didn't they once cry 'All hail!' to me? So Judas did to Christ. But Christ, out of twelve, found all loyal but one; I, out of twelve thousand, found none. God save the King! Won't anyone say amen? Am I both the priest and the clerk who answers him? Well then, amen. God save the King, although I am not him; and yet, amen, if heaven thinks he is me. What service have I been sent for to do here?
To do that office of thine own good will / Which tired majesty did make thee offer, / The resignation of thy state and crown / To Henry Bolingbroke.
To carry out, of your own free will, what your weary majesty made you offer: to hand over your royal power and crown to Henry Bolingbroke.

Give me the crown. Here, cousin, seize the crown. / Here, cousin, / On this side my hand, and on that side thine. / Now is this golden crown like a deep well / That owes two buckets, filling one another; / The emptier ever dancing in the air, / The other down, unseen, and full of water. / That bucket down and full of tears am I, / Drinking my griefs, whilst you mount up on high.

Give me the crown. Here, cousin, take hold of the crown. Here, cousin: my hand on this side, and yours on that. Now this golden crown is like a deep well with two buckets, filling each other in turn, the emptier one always dancing in the air, the other one down below, unseen and full of water. I am that bucket, down and full of tears, drinking my griefs while you rise up high.
I thought you had been willing to resign.
I thought you were willing to give up the crown.
My crown I am; but still my griefs are mine. / You may my glories and my state depose, / But not my griefs; still am I king of those.
My crown I am; but my griefs are still mine. You may depose my glory and my royal power, but not my griefs. I am still king of those.
Part of your cares you give me with your crown.
With your crown you give me part of your cares.

Your cares set up do not pluck my cares down. / My care is loss of care, by old care done; / Your care is gain of care, by new care won. / The cares I give I have, though given away; / They tend the crown, yet still with me they stay.

Your cares being raised up don't take my cares down. My care is the loss of care, caused by my old carelessness. Your care is the gain of care, won by new effort. The cares I give I still have, though I give them away. They wait on the crown, and yet they stay with me.
Are you contented to resign the crown?
Are you willing to give up the crown?

Ay, no; no, ay; for I must nothing be; / Therefore no no, for I resign to thee. / Now mark me how I will undo myself: / I give this heavy weight from off my head, / And this unwieldy sceptre from my hand, / The pride of kingly sway from out my heart; / With mine own tears I wash away my balm, / With mine own hands I give away my crown, / With mine own tongue deny my sacred state, / With mine own breath release all duteous rites: / All pomp and majesty I do forswear; / My manors, rents, revenues, I forgo; / My acts, decrees, and statutes, I deny: / God pardon all oaths that are broke to me! / God keep all vows unbroke are made to thee! / Make me, that nothing have, with nothing griev'd, / And thou with all pleas'd, that hast all achiev'd! / Long mayst thou live in Richard's seat to sit, / And soon lie Richard in an earthly pit! / God save King Henry, unking'd Richard says, / And send him many years of sunshine days! / What more remains?

Yes, no; no, yes. Because I must be nothing, I can't say no; I give it up to you. Now watch how I will undo myself. I take this heavy weight off my head and this clumsy sceptre out of my hand, and the pride of royal power out of my heart. With my own tears I wash off my holy oil. With my own hands I give away my crown. With my own tongue I deny my sacred rank. With my own breath I release everyone from their duties. I give up all pomp and majesty. I give up my estates, rents and income. I cancel my acts, decrees and laws. God forgive all the oaths that are broken to me! God keep unbroken all the vows that are made to you! Make me, who have nothing, not grieve about having nothing, and make you, who have gained everything, pleased with everything! Long may you live to sit on Richard's throne, and may Richard soon lie in a hole in the earth! God save King Henry, says Richard, no longer king, and send him many years of sunny days! What else is there?

[Offering a paper] No more, but that you read / These accusations, and these grievous crimes / Committed by your person and your followers / Against the state and profit of this land; / That, by confessing them, the souls of men / May deem that you are worthily depos'd.

Nothing more, except that you read out these charges and the serious crimes committed by you and your followers against the state and welfare of this country, so that by your confessing them people will believe you have been rightly deposed.

Must I do so? And must I ravel out / My weav'd-up follies? Gentle Northumberland, / If thy offences were upon record, / Would it not shame thee in so fair a troop / To read a lecture of them? If thou wouldst, / There shouldst thou find one heinous article, / Containing the deposing of a king / And cracking the strong warrant of an oath, / Mark'd with a blot, damn'd in the book of heaven. / Nay, all of you that stand and look upon me / Whilst that my wretchedness doth bait myself, / Though some of you, with Pilate, wash your hands, / Showing an outward pity; yet you Pilates / Have here deliver'd me to my sour cross, / And water cannot wash away your sin.

Must I do that? Must I unpick the woven pattern of my follies? Gentle Northumberland, if your crimes were written down, wouldn't you be ashamed to read them out in front of such a fine company? If you did, you would find there one terrible charge: the deposing of a king and the breaking of the strong bond of an oath, marked with a black stain and damned in the book of heaven. No, all of you who stand looking at me while my misery torments me, though some of you wash your hands like Pilate, showing pity on the outside, you Pilates have still handed me over to my bitter cross, and water cannot wash away your sin.
My lord, dispatch; read o'er these articles.
My lord, hurry. Read through these charges.

Mine eyes are full of tears; I cannot see: / And yet salt water blinds them not so much / But they can see a sort of traitors here. / Nay, if I turn mine eyes upon myself, / I find myself a traitor with the rest; / For I have given here my soul's consent / T'undeck the pompous body of a king; / Made glory base, and sovereignty a slave, / Proud majesty a subject, state a peasant.

My eyes are full of tears; I can't see. And yet the salt water doesn't blind them so much that they can't see a pack of traitors here. No, if I turn my eyes on myself, I find I am a traitor along with the rest, because I have given my soul's agreement here to strip the splendid body of a king, to make glory lowly and royal power a slave, proud majesty a subject and kingship a peasant.

No lord of thine, thou haught insulting man, / Nor no man's lord; I have no name, no title, / No, not that name was given me at the font, / But 'tis usurp'd: alack the heavy day! / That I have worn so many winters out, / And know not now what name to call myself! / O! that I were a mockery king of snow, / Standing before the sun of Bolingbroke / To melt myself away in water-drops! / Good king, great king,—and yet not greatly good, / An if my word be sterling yet in England, / Let it command a mirror hither straight, / That it may show me what a face I have, / Since it is bankrupt of his majesty.

I'm no lord of yours, you proud, insulting man, and no man's lord. I have no name, no title; no, not even the name I was given at my christening, because that has been taken from me. Alas, what a sad day, that I have lived through so many winters and don't know now what name to call myself! Oh, I wish I were a snowman king, standing in front of the sun of Bolingbroke to melt myself away in drops of water! Good king, great king, though not greatly good, if my word is still worth anything in England, let it order a mirror to be brought here at once, so that it can show me what my face looks like now that it has lost its majesty.
Go some of you and fetch a looking-glass.
Some of you go and fetch a mirror.
Read o'er this paper while the glass doth come.
Read through this paper while the mirror is coming.
Fiend! thou torments me ere I come to hell.
Devil! You torment me before I even get to hell.
Urge it no more, my Lord Northumberland.
Don't press it any further, my Lord Northumberland.
The Commons will not then be satisfied.
Then the Commons won't be satisfied.
They shall be satisfied; I'll read enough, / When I do see the very book indeed / Where all my sins are writ, and that's myself.
They will be satisfied. I'll read enough when I see the real book where all my sins are written, and that's myself.

Give me that glass, and therein will I read. / No deeper wrinkles yet? Hath sorrow struck / So many blows upon this face of mine / And made no deeper wounds? O flatt'ring glass! / Like to my followers in prosperity, / Thou dost beguile me. Was this face the face / That every day under his household roof / Did keep ten thousand men? Was this the face / That like the sun did make beholders wink? / Is this the face which fac'd so many follies / That was at last out-fac'd by Bolingbroke? / A brittle glory shineth in this face: / As brittle as the glory is the face;

Give me that mirror, and I will read in it. No deeper wrinkles yet? Has sorrow struck so many blows on this face of mine and made no deeper wounds? Oh, flattering mirror! You deceive me, like my followers when I was doing well. Was this the face that every day fed ten thousand men under its roof? Was this the face that, like the sun, made people who looked at it blink? Is this the face that put a bold face on so many follies, and was at last outfaced by Bolingbroke? A fragile glory shines in this face. The face is as fragile as the glory.
For there it is, crack'd in a hundred shivers. / Mark, silent king, the moral of this sport, / How soon my sorrow hath destroy'd my face.
Because there it is, cracked into a hundred pieces. Notice, silent king, the moral of this game: how quickly my sorrow has destroyed my face.
The shadow of your sorrow hath destroy'd / The shadow of your face.
The shadow of your sorrow has destroyed the shadow of your face.

Say that again. / The shadow of my sorrow! Ha! let's see: / 'Tis very true: my grief lies all within; / And these external manner of laments / Are merely shadows to the unseen grief / That swells with silence in the tortur'd soul. / There lies the substance: and I thank thee, king, / For thy great bounty, that not only givest / Me cause to wail, but teachest me the way / How to lament the cause. I'll beg one boon, / And then be gone and trouble you no more. / Shall I obtain it?

Say that again. The shadow of my sorrow! Ha! Let's see. It's very true. My grief is all inside, and these outward ways of mourning are only shadows of the unseen grief that swells in silence in my tortured soul. That's where the real thing is. And I thank you, king, for your great generosity, which not only gives me reason to weep but teaches me how to mourn that reason. I'll ask one favour, and then go and trouble you no more. Shall I have it?

'Fair cousin'! I am greater than a king; / For when I was a king, my flatterers / Were then but subjects; being now a subject, / I have a king here to my flatterer. / Being so great, I have no need to beg.
'Fair cousin'! I am greater than a king. When I was a king, my flatterers were only subjects. Now that I am a subject, I have a king here as my flatterer. Being so great, I have no need to beg.
Then give me leave to go.
Whither you will, so I were from your sights.
Wherever you like, as long as I am out of your sight.
Go, some of you convey him to the Tower.
Some of you, take him to the Tower.
O, good! convey? conveyers are you all, / That rise thus nimbly by a true king's fall.
Oh, good! 'Take'? You are all takers, thieves who rise so quickly through a true king's fall.
On Wednesday next we solemnly set down / Our coronation: lords, prepare yourselves.
We formally set our coronation for next Wednesday. Lords, get yourselves ready.
A woeful pageant have we here beheld.
We have seen a sad show here.
The woe's to come; the children yet unborn / Shall feel this day as sharp to them as thorn.
The sorrow is still to come. Children not yet born will feel this day as sharply as a thorn.
You holy clergymen, is there no plot / To rid the realm of this pernicious blot?
You holy clergymen, is there no plan to rid the country of this destructive stain?

My lord, / Before I freely speak my mind herein, / You shall not only take the sacrament / To bury mine intents, but also to effect / Whatever I shall happen to devise. / I see your brows are full of discontent, / Your hearts of sorrow, and your eyes of tears: / Come home with me to supper; I will lay / A plot shall show us all a merry day.

My lord, before I speak my mind freely on this, you must take communion and swear not only to keep my intentions secret, but also to carry out whatever I decide. I can see your brows are full of discontent, your hearts full of sorrow and your eyes full of tears. Come home to supper with me. I will set out a plan that will bring us all a happy day.

This way the King will come; this is the way / To Julius Caesar's ill-erected tower, / To whose flint bosom my condemned lord / Is doom'd a prisoner by proud Bolingbroke. / Here let us rest, if this rebellious earth / Have any resting for her true King's queen.

The King will come this way. This is the way to the Tower that Julius Caesar built for evil, where proud Bolingbroke has sentenced my condemned husband to be a prisoner in its flint-hard heart. Let's rest here, if this rebellious earth has any resting place for her true King's queen.

But soft, but see, or rather do not see, / My fair rose wither; yet look up, behold, / That you in pity may dissolve to dew, / And wash him fresh again with true-love tears. / Ah! thou, the model where old Troy did stand; / Thou map of honour, thou King Richard's tomb, / And not King Richard; thou most beauteous inn, / Why should hard-favour'd grief be lodg'd in thee, / When triumph is become an alehouse guest?

But wait, look, or rather don't look, at my fair rose withering. And yet look up, see him, so that you melt into dew out of pity and wash him fresh again with tears of true love. Ah, you, the ruin where old Troy once stood, the outline of honour, King Richard's tomb and not King Richard himself, you most beautiful inn, why should ugly grief be lodged in you, when triumph has become a guest at a common alehouse?

Join not with grief, fair woman, do not so, / To make my end too sudden: learn, good soul, / To think our former state a happy dream; / From which awak'd, the truth of what we are / Shows us but this. I am sworn brother, sweet, / To grim Necessity; and he and I / Will keep a league till death. Hie thee to France, / And cloister thee in some religious house: / Our holy lives must win a new world's crown, / Which our profane hours here have thrown down.

Don't join forces with grief, fair woman, don't, to make my end too sudden. Learn, good soul, to think of our former greatness as a happy dream. Now that we have woken from it, the truth of what we are shows us only this. I am sworn brother, sweet, to grim Necessity, and he and I will stay allied until death. Hurry to France and shut yourself away in some convent. Our holy lives must win a crown in the next world, which our wicked hours here have thrown down.

What! is my Richard both in shape and mind / Transform'd and weaken'd! Hath Bolingbroke depos'd / Thine intellect? Hath he been in thy heart? / The lion dying thrusteth forth his paw / And wounds the earth, if nothing else, with rage / To be o'erpower'd; and wilt thou, pupil-like, / Take the correction mildly, kiss the rod, / And fawn on rage with base humility, / Which art a lion and the king of beasts?

What! Has my Richard been changed and weakened in both body and mind? Has Bolingbroke deposed your mind too? Has he been inside your heart? The lion, when he is dying, thrusts out his paw and wounds the earth, if nothing else, in rage at being overpowered. And will you, like a schoolboy, take your punishment meekly, kiss the cane and fawn on the anger against you with low humility, when you are a lion and the king of beasts?

A king of beasts, indeed; if aught but beasts, / I had been still a happy king of men. / Good sometimes queen, prepare thee hence for France. / Think I am dead, and that even here thou tak'st, / As from my death-bed, thy last living leave. / In winter's tedious nights sit by the fire / With good old folks, and let them tell thee tales / Of woeful ages long ago betid; / And ere thou bid good night, to quit their griefs / Tell thou the lamentable tale of me, / And send the hearers weeping to their beds; / For why, the senseless brands will sympathize / The heavy accent of thy moving tongue, / And in compassion weep the fire out; / And some will mourn in ashes, some coal-black, / For the deposing of a rightful king.

King of beasts indeed. If they had been anything but beasts, I would still be a happy king of men. Good woman, once my queen, get ready to leave for France. Think I am dead, and that even here you are taking your last leave of me, as if at my deathbed. On long winter nights, sit by the fire with good old people and let them tell you stories of sad times long ago. And before you say good night, to pay them back for their sad stories, tell them the sad story of me, and send your listeners weeping to their beds. Because even the senseless logs will feel for the heavy tone of your moving voice and weep the fire out in pity, and some will mourn in ashes, some in coal-black, for the deposing of a rightful king.
My lord, the mind of Bolingbroke is chang'd; / You must to Pomfret, not unto the Tower. / And, madam, there is order ta'en for you: / With all swift speed you must away to France.
My lord, Bolingbroke has changed his mind. You must go to Pomfret, not to the Tower. And, madam, arrangements have been made for you: you must leave for France as fast as possible.

Northumberland, thou ladder wherewithal / The mounting Bolingbroke ascends my throne, / The time shall not be many hours of age / More than it is, ere foul sin gathering head / Shall break into corruption. Thou shalt think, / Though he divide the realm and give thee half / It is too little, helping him to all; / And he shall think that thou, which know'st the way / To plant unrightful kings, wilt know again, / Being ne'er so little urg'd, another way / To pluck him headlong from the usurped throne. / The love of wicked men converts to fear; / That fear to hate; and hate turns one or both / To worthy danger and deserved death.

Northumberland, you ladder that the climbing Bolingbroke uses to reach my throne, it won't be many hours older than it is now before foul sin comes to a head and bursts like a boil. You will think, even if he divides the kingdom and gives you half, that it is too little, since you helped him get all of it. And he will think that you, who know how to set up kings who have no right, will know another way, with very little pushing, to pull him headlong off the throne he stole. The love of wicked men turns to fear, that fear to hate, and hate leads one or both of them to the danger and death they deserve.
My guilt be on my head, and there an end. / Take leave, and part; for you must part forthwith.
Let my guilt be on my own head, and that's the end of it. Say goodbye and part, because you must part immediately.

Doubly divorc'd! Bad men, ye violate / A twofold marriage; 'twixt my crown and me, / And then betwixt me and my married wife. / Let me unkiss the oath 'twixt thee and me; / And yet not so, for with a kiss 'twas made. / Part us, Northumberland: I towards the north, / Where shivering cold and sickness pines the clime; / My wife to France, from whence set forth in pomp, / She came adorned hither like sweet May, / Sent back like Hallowmas or short'st of day.

Divorced twice over! Wicked men, you break two marriages: between my crown and me, and then between me and my wife. Let me unkiss the vow between you and me. And yet no, because it was made with a kiss. Separate us, Northumberland: me to the north, where shivering cold and sickness waste the land; my wife to France, where she came from in splendour, decked out like sweet May, and is sent back like dark November, the shortest day of the year.
And must we be divided? Must we part?
And must we be divided? Must we part?
Ay, hand from hand, my love, and heart from heart.
Yes, hand from hand, my love, and heart from heart.
Banish us both, and send the king with me.
Banish us both, and send the king with me.
That were some love, but little policy.
That would be loving, but not good politics.
Then whither he goes, thither let me go.
Then wherever he goes, let me go there too.
So two, together weeping, make one woe. / Weep thou for me in France, I for thee here; / Better far off than near, be ne'er the near. / Go, count thy way with sighs; I mine with groans.

Then two, weeping together, make one sorrow. You weep for me in France, and I for you here. It is better to be far apart than near if we can never be any nearer. Go, and measure your road with sighs; I'll measure mine with groans.
So longest way shall have the longest moans.
Then the longest road will have the longest moans.

Twice for one step I'll groan, the way being short, / And piece the way out with a heavy heart. / Come, come, in wooing sorrow let's be brief, / Since, wedding it, there is such length in grief. / One kiss shall stop our mouths, and dumbly part; / Thus give I mine, and thus take I thy heart.

I'll groan twice for every step, since my road is short, and make it longer with a heavy heart. Come, come, let's be brief in courting sorrow, since once we're married to it, grief lasts so long. One kiss will stop our mouths, and we'll part in silence. Like this I give you mine, and like this I take your heart.
Give me mine own again; 'twere no good part / To take on me to keep and kill thy heart.
Give me my own back. It would be a bad thing to take your heart to keep and then kill it with grief.
So, now I have mine own again, be gone. / That I may strive to kill it with a groan.
There, now I have my own again. Go, so that I can try to kill it with a groan.
We make woe wanton with this fond delay: / Once more, adieu; the rest let sorrow say.
We play with sorrow by this foolish delay. Once more, goodbye. Let sorrow say the rest.
My Lord, you told me you would tell the rest, / When weeping made you break the story off, / Of our two cousins' coming into London.
My lord, you told me you would tell me the rest of the story of our two nephews' arrival in London, when crying made you break off.
At that sad stop, my lord, / Where rude misgoverned hands from windows' tops / Threw dust and rubbish on King Richard's head.
At that sad point, my lord, where rough, unruly hands at the tops of windows threw dust and rubbish on King Richard's head.

Then, as I said, the Duke, great Bolingbroke, / Mounted upon a hot and fiery steed / Which his aspiring rider seem'd to know, / With slow but stately pace kept on his course, / Whilst all tongues cried 'God save thee, Bolingbroke!' / You would have thought the very windows spake, / So many greedy looks of young and old / Through casements darted their desiring eyes / Upon his visage; and that all the walls / With painted imagery had said at once / 'Jesu preserve thee! Welcome, Bolingbroke!' / Whilst he, from the one side to the other turning, / Bareheaded, lower than his proud steed's neck, / Bespake them thus, 'I thank you, countrymen:' / And thus still doing, thus he pass'd along.

Then, as I said, the Duke, great Bolingbroke, riding a hot, fiery horse that seemed to know its ambitious rider, kept on his way at a slow but stately pace, while everyone shouted, 'God save you, Bolingbroke!' You would have thought the windows themselves were speaking, so many eager eyes of young and old darted their longing looks through them at his face; and that all the walls, hung with painted cloths, were saying at once, 'Jesus protect you! Welcome, Bolingbroke!' Meanwhile he, turning from one side to the other, with his head bare and bowed lower than his proud horse's neck, spoke to them like this: 'Thank you, countrymen.' And doing this all the way, he passed along.
Alack, poor Richard! where rode he the whilst?
Alas, poor Richard! Where was he riding all this time?

As in a theatre, the eyes of men / After a well-grac'd actor leaves the stage / Are idly bent on him that enters next, / Thinking his prattle to be tedious; / Even so, or with much more contempt, men's eyes / Did scowl on Richard: no man cried 'God save him;' / No joyful tongue gave him his welcome home; / But dust was thrown upon his sacred head, / Which with such gentle sorrow he shook off, / His face still combating with tears and smiles, / The badges of his grief and patience, / That had not God, for some strong purpose, steel'd / The hearts of men, they must perforce have melted, / And barbarism itself have pitied him. / But heaven hath a hand in these events, / To whose high will we bound our calm contents. / To Bolingbroke are we sworn subjects now, / Whose state and honour I for aye allow.

As in a theatre, when a popular actor leaves the stage, people's eyes turn carelessly to the one who comes on next, thinking his chatter boring; in the same way, or with much more contempt, people's eyes scowled at Richard. No one shouted 'God save him'. No joyful voice welcomed him home. Instead dust was thrown on his sacred head, which he shook off with such gentle sorrow, his face struggling between tears and smiles, the signs of his grief and his patience, that if God had not hardened men's hearts for some strong purpose, they would have had to melt, and even savages would have pitied him. But heaven has a hand in these events, and we limit our wishes calmly to its high will. We are sworn subjects of Bolingbroke now, and I accept his power and honour for ever.
Aumerle that was; / But that is lost for being Richard's friend, / And madam, you must call him Rutland now. / I am in Parliament pledge for his truth / And lasting fealty to the new-made king.

Aumerle he was; but he has lost that title for being Richard's friend, and, madam, you must call him Rutland now. I have pledged myself in Parliament as guarantee of his loyalty and lasting faithfulness to the new king.
Welcome, my son: who are the violets now / That strew the green lap of the new come spring?
Welcome, my son. Who are the violets now that cover the green lap of the newly arrived spring?
Madam, I know not, nor I greatly care not. / God knows I had as lief be none as one.
Madam, I don't know, and I don't much care. God knows I'd as soon not be one as be one.
Well, bear you well in this new spring of time, / Lest you be cropp'd before you come to prime. / What news from Oxford? hold those justs and triumphs?
Well, behave yourself well in this new spring of time, or you may be cut down before you come into flower. What news from Oxford? Are those tournaments and celebrations still going ahead?
For aught I know, my lord, they do.
As far as I know, my lord, they are.
You will be there, I know.
You will be there, I know.
If God prevent not, I purpose so.
If God doesn't prevent it, I intend to be.
What seal is that hangs without thy bosom? / Yea, look'st thou pale? Let me see the writing.
What seal is that hanging outside your coat? What, are you going pale? Let me see the writing.
No matter, then, who see it. / I will be satisfied; let me see the writing.
Then it doesn't matter who sees it. I will be satisfied. Let me see the writing.
I do beseech your Grace to pardon me; / It is a matter of small consequence / Which for some reasons I would not have seen.
I beg your Grace to excuse me. It's something unimportant that, for certain reasons, I don't want anyone to see.
Which for some reasons, sir, I mean to see. / I fear, I fear—
And for certain reasons, sir, I mean to see it. I fear, I fear...
What should you fear? / 'Tis nothing but some bond that he is ent'red into / For gay apparel 'gainst the triumph day.
What should you be afraid of? It's only some IOU he has signed for fine clothes for the day of the tournament.
Bound to himself! What doth he with a bond / That he is bound to? Wife, thou art a fool. / Boy, let me see the writing.
Owed to himself? What is he doing with an IOU that he holds himself? Wife, you're a fool. Boy, let me see the writing.
I do beseech you, pardon me; I may not show it.
I beg you, excuse me. I can't show it.
I will be satisfied; let me see it, I say.
I will be satisfied. Let me see it, I say.
Treason, foul treason! Villain! traitor! slave!
Treason, foul treason! Villain! Traitor! Wretch!
What is the matter, my lord?
Saddle my horse. / God for his mercy! what treachery is here!
Saddle my horse. God have mercy! What treachery is this!
Why, what is it, my lord?
Why, what is it, my lord?
Give me my boots, I say; saddle my horse. / Now, by mine honour, by my life, my troth, / I will appeach the villain.
Give me my boots, I tell you. Saddle my horse. Now, by my honour, by my life, by my faith, I will denounce the villain.
I will not peace. What is the matter, Aumerle?
I won't be quiet. What's the matter, Aumerle?
Good mother, be content; it is no more / Than my poor life must answer.
Good mother, calm down. It's nothing more than my poor life will have to pay for.
Bring me my boots. I will unto the King.
Bring me my boots. I'm going to the King.
Strike him, Aumerle. Poor boy, thou art amaz'd.
Hit him, Aumerle. Poor boy, you're stunned.
Hence, villain! never more come in my sight.
Get out, villain! Never come into my sight again.
Give me my boots, I say.
Give me my boots, I tell you.

Why, York, what wilt thou do? / Wilt thou not hide the trespass of thine own? / Have we more sons? or are we like to have? / Is not my teeming date drunk up with time? / And wilt thou pluck my fair son from mine age / And rob me of a happy mother's name? / Is he not like thee? Is he not thine own?

Why, York, what are you going to do? Won't you hide your own son's crime? Do we have any more sons, or are we likely to? Hasn't time used up my years for having children? And will you snatch my fair son away from me in my old age and rob me of the name of happy mother? Isn't he like you? Isn't he your own?
Thou fond mad woman, / Wilt thou conceal this dark conspiracy? / A dozen of them here have ta'en the sacrament, / And interchangeably set down their hands / To kill the King at Oxford.
You foolish, mad woman, do you want to hide this dark conspiracy? A dozen of them have taken communion and signed their names to each other's copies to kill the King at Oxford.
He shall be none; / We'll keep him here: then what is that to him?
He won't be one of them. We'll keep him here. Then what has it got to do with him?
Away, fond woman! were he twenty times my son / I would appeach him.
Away, foolish woman! If he were my son twenty times over, I would denounce him.

Hadst thou groan'd for him / As I have done, thou'dst be more pitiful. / But now I know thy mind: thou dost suspect / That I have been disloyal to thy bed / And that he is a bastard, not thy son: / Sweet York, sweet husband, be not of that mind. / He is as like thee as a man may be / Not like to me, or any of my kin, / And yet I love him.

If you had groaned in labour for him as I did, you would have more pity. But now I know what you think. You suspect that I have been unfaithful to you, and that he is a bastard, not your son. Sweet York, sweet husband, don't think that. He is as like you as any man can be, not like me or any of my family. And yet I love him.
Get out of my way, unruly woman!

After, Aumerle! Mount thee upon his horse; / Spur post, and get before him to the king, / And beg thy pardon ere he do accuse thee. / I'll not be long behind; though I be old, / I doubt not but to ride as fast as York: / And never will I rise up from the ground / Till Bolingbroke have pardon'd thee. Away! be gone.

After him, Aumerle! Get on his horse, spur it as fast as you can and get to the king before him, and beg for your pardon before he accuses you. I won't be far behind. Though I'm old, I'm sure I can ride as fast as York. And I will never get up off the ground until Bolingbroke has pardoned you. Go! Away!

Can no man tell me of my unthrifty son? / 'Tis full three months since I did see him last. / If any plague hang over us, 'tis he. / I would to God, my lords, he might be found. / Inquire at London, 'mongst the taverns there, / For there, they say, he daily doth frequent / With unrestrained loose companions, / Even such, they say, as stand in narrow lanes / And beat our watch and rob our passengers; / Which he, young wanton and effeminate boy, / Takes on the point of honour to support / So dissolute a crew.

Can nobody tell me anything about my wild son? It's three whole months since I last saw him. If any disaster is hanging over us, it's him. I wish to God, my lords, he could be found. Ask in London, among the taverns there, because they say he goes there every day with wild, unruly companions, the kind, they say, who wait in narrow alleys to beat up our watchmen and rob travellers; while he, a spoiled, soft young man, makes it a point of honour to support such a disgraceful gang.
My lord, some two days since I saw the prince, / And told him of those triumphs held at Oxford.
My lord, about two days ago I saw the prince and told him about the tournament being held at Oxford.
And what did the young gallant say?
His answer was: he would unto the stews, / And from the common'st creature pluck a glove / And wear it as a favour; and with that / He would unhorse the lustiest challenger.
He answered that he would go to the brothels, take a glove from the commonest whore there and wear it as a lady's token, and with that he would knock the strongest challenger off his horse.
As dissolute as desperate; yet through both / I see some sparks of better hope, which elder years / May happily bring forth. But who comes here?
As wild as he is reckless. And yet through both I see some sparks of better hope, which older age may luckily bring out. But who is this?
What means our cousin that he stares and looks / So wildly?
What does our cousin mean by staring and looking so wild?
God save your Grace! I do beseech your majesty, / To have some conference with your Grace alone.
God save your Grace! I beg your majesty to let me talk with your Grace alone.
Withdraw yourselves, and leave us here alone.
Leave us, and let us be alone here.
What is the matter with our cousin now?
What's the matter with our cousin now?
[Kneels] For ever may my knees grow to the earth, / My tongue cleave to my roof within my mouth, / Unless a pardon ere I rise or speak.
May my knees grow into the earth for ever, and my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth, unless I have a pardon before I get up or speak.
Intended or committed was this fault? / If on the first, how heinous e'er it be, / To win thy after-love I pardon thee.
Was this crime planned or carried out? If only planned, however terrible it is, I pardon you to win your love afterwards.
Then give me leave that I may turn the key, / That no man enter till my tale be done.
Then let me turn the key, so that no one comes in until I have finished my story.
[Within] My liege, beware! look to thyself; / Thou hast a traitor in thy presence there.
My lord, beware! Look after yourself. You have a traitor there with you.
Villain, I'll make sure you can do no harm.
Stay thy revengeful hand; thou hast no cause to fear.
Hold back your revengeful hand. You have no reason to be afraid.
[Within] Open the door, secure, foolhardy king: / Shall I, for love, speak treason to thy face? / Open the door, or I will break it open.
Open the door, you careless, foolhardy king. Must I, out of love, speak treason to your face? Open the door, or I'll break it open.
What is the matter, uncle? speak; / Recover breath; tell us how near is danger, / That we may arm us to encounter it.
What's the matter, uncle? Speak. Get your breath back. Tell us how near the danger is, so that we can arm ourselves to meet it.
Peruse this writing here, and thou shalt know / The treason that my haste forbids me show.
Read this paper here, and you will know about the treason that I am too out of breath to explain.
Remember, as thou read'st, thy promise pass'd: / I do repent me; read not my name there; / My heart is not confederate with my hand.
Remember your promise as you read. I repent. Don't read my name there. My heart isn't partner to my hand.

It was, villain, ere thy hand did set it down. / I tore it from the traitor's bosom, king; / Fear, and not love, begets his penitence. / Forget to pity him, lest thy pity prove / A serpent that will sting thee to the heart.

It was, villain, before your hand wrote it down. I tore it out of the traitor's coat, King. Fear, not love, makes him sorry. Forget to pity him, or your pity may turn out to be a snake that stings you to the heart.

O heinous, strong, and bold conspiracy! / O loyal father of a treacherous son! / Thou sheer, immaculate, and silver fountain, / From whence this stream through muddy passages / Hath held his current and defil'd himself! / Thy overflow of good converts to bad; / And thy abundant goodness shall excuse / This deadly blot in thy digressing son.

Oh, terrible, powerful and bold conspiracy! Oh, loyal father of a treacherous son! You pure, spotless, silver spring, from which this stream has run through muddy channels and dirtied itself! Your overflowing goodness turns into bad in him, and your great goodness will excuse this deadly stain in your straying son.

So shall my virtue be his vice's bawd, / And he shall spend mine honour with his shame, / As thriftless sons their scraping fathers' gold. / Mine honour lives when his dishonour dies, / Or my sham'd life in his dishonour lies: / Thou kill'st me in his life; giving him breath, / The traitor lives, the true man's put to death.

Then my virtue will be the pimp for his vice, and he will spend my honour on his shame, as wasteful sons spend their stingy fathers' gold. My honour lives when his dishonour dies, or else my shamed life lies in his dishonour. You kill me by letting him live. If you give him breath, the traitor lives and the loyal man is put to death.
[Within] What ho! my liege, for God's sake, let me in.
Hello there! My lord, for God's sake, let me in.
What shrill-voic'd suppliant makes this eager cry?
What shrill-voiced beggar is crying out so eagerly?
[Within] A woman, and thine aunt, great king; 'tis I. / Speak with me, pity me, open the door: / A beggar begs that never begg'd before.
A woman, and your aunt, great king. It's me. Speak to me, pity me, open the door. A beggar is begging who has never begged before.
Our scene is alter'd from a serious thing, / And now chang'd to 'The Beggar and the King.' / My dangerous cousin, let your mother in: / I know she's come to pray for your foul sin.
Our play has changed from a serious drama into 'The Beggar and the King'. My dangerous cousin, let your mother in. I know she has come to plead for your foul sin.
If thou do pardon, whosoever pray, / More sins for this forgiveness prosper may. / This fester'd joint cut off, the rest rest sound; / This let alone will all the rest confound.
If you pardon him, whoever pleads, more sins may grow because of this forgiveness. Cut off this infected limb, and the rest stays healthy. Leave it alone, and it will destroy all the rest.
O King, believe not this hard-hearted man: / Love, loving not itself, none other can.
O King, don't believe this hard-hearted man. Someone who doesn't love his own flesh and blood can't love anyone else.
Thou frantic woman, what dost thou make here? / Shall thy old dugs once more a traitor rear?
You crazy woman, what are you doing here? Will your old breasts feed a traitor once again?
Sweet York, be patient. [Kneels] Hear me, gentle liege.
Sweet York, be patient. Hear me, gentle lord.
Not yet, I thee beseech. / For ever will I walk upon my knees, / And never see day that the happy sees, / Till thou give joy: until thou bid me joy / By pardoning Rutland, my transgressing boy.
Not yet, I beg you. I will walk on my knees for ever and never see a happy day until you give me joy, by pardoning Rutland, my sinful boy.
Unto my mother's prayers I bend my knee.
I kneel to support my mother's prayers.
Against them both, my true joints bended be.
And I bend my loyal knees against them both.
Ill mayst thou thrive, if thou grant any grace!
May bad luck come to you if you grant any mercy!

Pleads he in earnest? Look upon his face; / His eyes do drop no tears, his prayers are in jest; / His words come from his mouth, ours from our breast; / He prays but faintly and would be denied; / We pray with heart and soul, and all beside: / His weary joints would gladly rise, I know; / Our knees still kneel till to the ground they grow: / His prayers are full of false hypocrisy; / Ours of true zeal and deep integrity. / Our prayers do out-pray his; then let them have / That mercy which true prayer ought to have.

Does he mean it? Look at his face. His eyes shed no tears; his prayers are a joke. His words come from his mouth, ours from our hearts. He prays weakly and wants to be refused. We pray with heart and soul and everything else. His tired joints would happily get up, I know. Our knees will keep kneeling until they grow into the ground. His prayers are full of false hypocrisy, ours of true passion and deep honesty. Our prayers outpray his, so let them have the mercy that true prayer deserves.

Nay, do not say 'stand up'; / Say 'pardon' first, and afterwards 'stand up'. / An if I were thy nurse, thy tongue to teach, / 'Pardon' should be the first word of thy speech. / I never long'd to hear a word till now; / Say 'pardon,' king; let pity teach thee how: / The word is short, but not so short as sweet; / No word like 'pardon' for kings' mouths so meet.

No, don't say 'stand up'. Say 'pardon' first, and 'stand up' afterwards. If I were your nurse, teaching you to speak, 'pardon' would be the first word you said. I have never longed to hear a word until now. Say 'pardon', king. Let pity teach you how. The word is short, but even more sweet than short. No word is so fitting for kings' mouths as 'pardon'.
Speak it in French, King, say 'pardonne moy.'
Say it in French, King: say 'pardonne-moi', the polite way of saying no.

Dost thou teach pardon pardon to destroy? / Ah! my sour husband, my hard-hearted lord, / That sett'st the word itself against the word. / Speak 'pardon' as 'tis current in our land; / The chopping French we do not understand. / Thine eye begins to speak, set thy tongue there, / Or in thy piteous heart plant thou thine ear, / That hearing how our plaints and prayers do pierce, / Pity may move thee pardon to rehearse.

Are you teaching him to use the word 'pardon' to destroy pardon? Ah, my sour husband, my hard-hearted lord, who sets the word against itself! Say 'pardon' the way we use it in our country. We don't understand clipped French. Your eyes are beginning to speak; let your tongue say what they say. Or put your ear into your pitying heart, so that, hearing how our pleas and prayers pierce it, pity may move you to say 'pardon'.
I do not sue to stand; / Pardon is all the suit I have in hand.
I'm not begging to stand. Pardon is the only thing I'm asking for.
I pardon him, as God shall pardon me.
I pardon him, as God will pardon me.
O happy vantage of a kneeling knee! / Yet am I sick for fear: speak it again; / Twice saying 'pardon' doth not pardon twain,
Oh, what a happy result from kneeling! But I am still sick with fear. Say it again. Saying 'pardon' twice doesn't pardon two people,
but it makes one pardon strong.
With all my heart / I pardon him.
With all my heart I pardon him.
A god on earth thou art.
You are a god on earth.

But for our trusty brother-in-law and the abbot, / With all the rest of that consorted crew, / Destruction straight shall dog them at the heels. / Good uncle, help to order several powers / To Oxford, or where'er these traitors are: / They shall not live within this world, I swear, / But I will have them, if I once know where. / Uncle, farewell: and, cousin, adieu: / Your mother well hath pray'd, and prove you true.

But as for our trusty brother-in-law, the abbot and all the rest of that gang of conspirators, destruction will follow at their heels at once. Good uncle, help send several forces to Oxford or wherever these traitors are. I swear they won't stay alive in this world; I'll get them, once I know where they are. Uncle, goodbye. And, cousin, farewell. Your mother has prayed well; now prove yourself loyal.
Come, my old son: I pray God make thee new.
Come, my old son. I pray God makes you new.
Didst thou not mark the king, what words he spake? / 'Have I no friend will rid me of this living fear?' / Was it not so?
Didn't you notice what the king said? 'Have I no friend who will rid me of this living fear?' Wasn't that it?
'Have I no friend?' quoth he: he spake it twice / And urg'd it twice together, did he not?
'Have I no friend?' he said. He said it twice and pressed it twice in a row, didn't he?

And, speaking it, he wistly looked on me, / As who should say 'I would thou wert the man / That would divorce this terror from my heart'; / Meaning the king at Pomfret. Come, let's go. / I am the king's friend, and will rid his foe.

And as he said it, he looked at me meaningfully, as if to say, 'I wish you were the man who would free my heart of this terror', meaning the king at Pomfret. Come, let's go. I am the king's friend, and I'll get rid of his enemy.

I have been studying how I may compare / This prison where I live unto the world / And for because the world is populous, / And here is not a creature but myself, / I cannot do it; yet I'll hammer it out. / My brain I'll prove the female to my soul; / My soul the father: and these two beget / A generation of still-breeding thoughts, / And these same thoughts people this little world, / In humours like the people of this world, / For no thought is contented. The better sort, / As thoughts of things divine, are intermix'd / With scruples, and do set the word itself / Against the word: / As thus: 'Come, little ones'; and then again, / 'It is as hard to come as for a camel / To thread the postern of a needle's eye.' / Thoughts tending to ambition, they do plot / Unlikely wonders; how these vain weak nails / May tear a passage through the flinty ribs / Of this hard world, my ragged prison walls; / And, for they cannot, die in their own pride. / Thoughts tending to content flatter themselves / That they are not the first of fortune's slaves, / Nor shall not be the last; like silly beggars / Who sitting in the stocks refuge their shame, / That many have and others must sit there: / And in this thought they find a kind of ease, / Bearing their own misfortunes on the back / Of such as have before endur'd the like. / Thus play I in one person many people, / And none contented: sometimes am I king; / Then treasons make me wish myself a beggar, / And so I am: then crushing penury / Persuades me I was better when a king; / Then am I king'd again; and by and by / Think that I am unking'd by Bolingbroke, / And straight am nothing: but whate'er I be, / Nor I, nor any man that but man is / With nothing shall be pleas'd till he be eas'd / With being nothing. / Music do I hear? [Music] / Ha, ha! keep time. How sour sweet music is / When time is broke and no proportion kept! / So is it in the music of men's lives. / And here have I the daintiness of ear / To check time broke in a disorder'd string; / But, for the concord of my state and time, / Had not an ear to hear my true time broke. / I wasted time, and now doth time waste me; / For now hath time made me his numbering clock: / My thoughts are minutes; and with sighs they jar / Their watches on unto mine eyes, the outward watch, / Whereto my finger, like a dial's point, / Is pointing still, in cleansing them from tears. / Now sir, the sound that tells what hour it is / Are clamorous groans, which strike upon my heart, / Which is the bell: so sighs and tears and groans / Show minutes, times, and hours; but my time / Runs posting on in Bolingbroke's proud joy, / While I stand fooling here, his Jack o' the clock. / This music mads me; let it sound no more; / For though it have holp madmen to their wits, / In me it seems it will make wise men mad. / Yet blessing on his heart that gives it me! / For 'tis a sign of love; and love to Richard / Is a strange brooch in this all-hating world.

I have been working out how I can compare this prison where I live to the world. And because the world is full of people, and here there is no creature but me, I can't do it. But I'll hammer it out. I'll make my brain the mother and my soul the father, and the two of them will produce a family of thoughts that keep on breeding. And these same thoughts fill this little world, with moods like the people of this world, because no thought is satisfied. The better kind, like thoughts about religion, are mixed with doubts, and set one part of the Bible against another, like this: 'Come, little children', and then again, 'It is as hard to come to heaven as it is for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle.' Ambitious thoughts plan impossible wonders: how these useless, weak fingernails could tear a way through the flinty ribs of this hard world, my rough prison walls; and because they can't, they die in their own pride. Thoughts that tend towards contentment flatter themselves that they are not the first slaves of fortune and won't be the last, like simple beggars sitting in the stocks who comfort their shame by thinking that many have sat there before and others will have to. And in this thought they find a kind of relief, putting their own bad luck on the backs of those who have suffered the same before. So I play many people in one person, and none of them is content. Sometimes I am a king. Then treasons make me wish I were a beggar, and so I am. Then crushing poverty convinces me I was better off as a king; then I am king again; and soon I think that Bolingbroke has unkinged me, and at once I am nothing. But whatever I am, neither I nor any other man who is only a man will be pleased with anything until he is relieved by being nothing. Do I hear music? Ha, ha! Keep time. How sour sweet music is when the rhythm is broken and the beat isn't kept! It's the same in the music of men's lives. And here I have a fine enough ear to correct a broken rhythm on an out-of-tune string; but for the harmony of my kingship and my time, I had no ear to hear my true time breaking. I wasted time, and now time wastes me, because now time has made me his clock. My thoughts are minutes, and with sighs they tick them on to my eyes, the outer clock face, where my finger, like the hand of a clock, keeps pointing as it wipes away tears. Now, sir, the sound that tells the hour is loud groans that strike my heart, which is the bell. So sighs, tears and groans show minutes, quarters and hours. But my time runs on fast in Bolingbroke's proud joy, while I stand here playing the fool, his little figure that strikes the clock. This music is driving me mad. Let it play no more. Though it has helped madmen back to their senses, in me it seems it will make wise men mad. Yet bless the heart of the person who plays it for me, because it is a sign of love, and love for Richard is a rare jewel in this all-hating world.

Thanks, noble peer; / The cheapest of us is ten groats too dear. / What art thou? and how comest thou hither, man, / Where no man never comes but that sad dog / That brings me food to make misfortune live?

Thank you, noble peer. The cheaper of us is overpriced by ten groats. Who are you? And how have you got here, man, where no one ever comes except that miserable dog who brings me food to keep misfortune alive?

I was a poor groom of thy stable, king, / When thou wert king; who, travelling towards York, / With much ado at length have gotten leave / To look upon my sometimes royal master's face. / O! how it yearn'd my heart when I beheld, / In London streets, that coronation day, / When Bolingbroke rode on roan Barbary, / That horse that thou so often hast bestrid, / That horse that I so carefully have dress'd.

I was a poor groom in your stable, king, when you were king. I am travelling to York, and with a lot of trouble I have at last got permission to see the face of my former royal master. Oh, how it hurt my heart to see, in the streets of London, on that coronation day, Bolingbroke riding on roan Barbary, the horse you rode so often, the horse I groomed so carefully!
Rode he on Barbary? Tell me, gentle friend, / How went he under him?
Did he ride on Barbary? Tell me, gentle friend, how did the horse go under him?
So proudly as if he disdain'd the ground.
As proudly as if he scorned the ground.

So proud that Bolingbroke was on his back! / That jade hath eat bread from my royal hand; / This hand hath made him proud with clapping him. / Would he not stumble? would he not fall down,— / Since pride must have a fall,—and break the neck / Of that proud man that did usurp his back? / Forgiveness, horse! Why do I rail on thee, / Since thou, created to be aw'd by man, / Wast born to bear? I was not made a horse; / And yet I bear a burden like an ass, / Spur-gall'd and tir'd by jauncing Bolingbroke.

So proud that Bolingbroke was on his back! That nag has eaten bread from my royal hand. This hand made him proud by patting him. Wouldn't he stumble? Wouldn't he fall down, since pride must have a fall, and break the neck of that proud man who stole his back? Forgive me, horse! Why do I abuse you, when you were created to be ruled by man and born to carry? I was not made a horse, and yet I carry a load like a donkey, rubbed raw by spurs and worn out by Bolingbroke bouncing on my back.
[To the Groom] Fellow, give place; here is no longer stay.
You, make way. You can't stay here any longer.
If thou love me, 'tis time thou wert away.
If you love me, it's time you went.
My tongue dares not, that my heart shall say.
What my tongue doesn't dare say, my heart will.
My lord, will't please you to fall to?
My lord, would you like to start eating?
Taste of it first as thou art wont to do.
Taste it first, as you usually do.
My lord, I dare not: Sir Pierce of Exton, / Who lately came from the king, commands the contrary.
My lord, I don't dare. Sir Pierce of Exton, who has just come from the king, orders me not to.
The devil take Henry of Lancaster and thee! / Patience is stale, and I am weary of it.
The devil take Henry of Lancaster, and you! Patience has gone stale, and I'm tired of it.
How now! What means death in this rude assault? / Villain, thy own hand yields thy death's instrument.
What's this! What does death mean by this violent attack? Villain, your own hand gives me the weapon for your death.
Go thou and fill another room in hell.
Go and fill another room in hell.

That hand shall burn in never-quenching fire / That staggers thus my person. Exton, thy fierce hand / Hath with the king's blood stain'd the king's own land. / Mount, mount, my soul! thy seat is up on high; / Whilst my gross flesh sinks downward, here to die.

The hand that knocks me down like this will burn in a fire that never goes out. Exton, your fierce hand has stained the king's own land with the king's blood. Rise, rise, my soul! Your seat is up high, while my heavy flesh sinks down to die here.

As full of valour as of royal blood: / Both have I spilt; O! would the deed were good; / For now the devil, that told me I did well, / Says that this deed is chronicled in hell. / This dead king to the living king I'll bear. / Take hence the rest, and give them burial here.

As full of courage as of royal blood. I have spilled both. Oh, I wish the deed were good! Because now the devil, who told me I did well, says that this deed is recorded in hell. I'll take this dead king to the living king. Take the rest away and bury them here.
Kind uncle York, the latest news we hear / Is that the rebels have consum'd with fire / Our town of Cicester in Gloucestershire; / But whether they be ta'en or slain we hear not.
Kind uncle York, the latest news we have is that the rebels have burned down our town of Cirencester in Gloucestershire; but we haven't heard whether they have been captured or killed.
Welcome, my lord. What is the news?
Welcome, my lord. What is the news?

First, to thy sacred state wish I all happiness. / The next news is: I have to London sent / The heads of Salisbury, Spencer, Blunt, and Kent. / The manner of their taking may appear / At large discoursed in this paper here.

First, I wish your sacred majesty every happiness. The next news is that I have sent the heads of Salisbury, Spencer, Blunt and Kent to London. How they were captured is described in full in this paper here.
We thank thee, gentle Percy, for thy pains; / And to thy worth will add right worthy gains.
Thank you, noble Percy, for your trouble. I will reward your worth with gifts that match it.
My lord, I have from Oxford sent to London / The heads of Brocas and Sir Bennet Seely, / Two of the dangerous consorted traitors / That sought at Oxford thy dire overthrow.
My lord, I have sent from Oxford to London the heads of Brocas and Sir Bennet Seely, two of the dangerous conspirators who planned your terrible downfall at Oxford.
Thy pains, Fitzwater, shall not be forgot; / Right noble is thy merit, well I wot.
Your efforts won't be forgotten, Fitzwater. Your service is truly noble, I know.

The grand conspirator, Abbot of Westminster, / With clog of conscience and sour melancholy, / Hath yielded up his body to the grave; / But here is Carlisle living, to abide / Thy kingly doom, and sentence of his pride.

The chief conspirator, the Abbot of Westminster, weighed down by his conscience and bitter depression, has given up his body to the grave. But here is Carlisle, alive, to wait for your royal judgement and the sentence his pride deserves.

Carlisle, this is your doom: / Choose out some secret place, some reverend room, / More than thou hast, and with it joy thy life; / So as thou livest in peace, die free from strife; / For though mine enemy thou hast ever been, / High sparks of honour in thee have I seen.

Carlisle, this is your sentence: choose some quiet place, some religious house, holier than the one you have, and enjoy your life there. As long as you live in peace, you can die free from trouble. Though you have always been my enemy, I have seen high sparks of honour in you.
Great king, within this coffin I present / Thy buried fear: herein all breathless lies / The mightiest of thy greatest enemies, / Richard of Bordeaux, by me hither brought.
Great king, in this coffin I present your buried fear. Here lies, without breath, the mightiest of your great enemies, Richard of Bordeaux, brought here by me.
Exton, I thank thee not; for thou hast wrought / A deed of slander with thy fatal hand / Upon my head and all this famous land.
Exton, I don't thank you, because with your deadly hand you have done a deed that will bring disgrace on my head and on all this famous country.
From your own mouth, my lord, did I this deed.
I did this deed on the orders of your own mouth, my lord.

They love not poison that do poison need, / Nor do I thee: though I did wish him dead, / I hate the murderer, love him murdered. / The guilt of conscience take thou for thy labour, / But neither my good word nor princely favour: / With Cain go wander thorough shade of night, / And never show thy head by day nor light. / Lords, I protest my soul is full of woe, / That blood should sprinkle me to make me grow: / Come, mourn with me for what I do lament, / And put on sullen black incontinent. / I'll make a voyage to the Holy Land, / To wash this blood off from my guilty hand. / March sadly after; grace my mournings here, / In weeping after this untimely bier.

Those who need poison don't love it, and I don't love you. Though I wished him dead, I hate the murderer and love the murdered man. Take a guilty conscience as your reward for your work, but not my good word or royal favour. Go and wander with Cain through the shadows of night, and never show your face by day or in light. Lords, I swear my soul is full of sorrow that blood should be sprinkled on me to make me grow. Come, mourn with me for what I mourn, and put on gloomy black at once. I'll make a voyage to the Holy Land to wash this blood off my guilty hand. March sadly after me. Honour my mourning here by weeping as you follow this coffin of a man who died before his time.
